Text Passage: As a matter of fact, very little of the tramp-monster will survive inquiry. Take the generally accepted idea that tramps are dangerous characters. Quite apart from experience, one can say A PRIORI that very few tramps are dangerous, because if they were dangerous they would be treated accordingly. A casual ward will often admit a hundred tramps in one night, and these are handled by a staff of at most three porters. A hundred ruffians could not be controlled by three unarmed men. Indeed, when one sees how tramps let themselves be bullied by the workhouse officials, it is obvious that they are the most docile, broken-spirited creatures imaginable. Or take the idea that all tramps are drunkardsÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂan idea ridiculous on the face of it. No doubt many tramps would drink if they got the chance, but in the nature of things they cannot get the chance. At this moment a pale watery stuff called beer is sevenpence a pint in England. To be drunk on it would cost at least half a crown, and a man who can command half a crown at all often is not a tramp. The idea that tramps are impudent social parasites (ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂsturdy beggarsÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ) is not absolutely unfounded, but it is only true in a few per cent of the cases. Deliberate, cynical parasitism, such as one reads of in Jack LondonÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂs books on American tramping, is not in the English character. The English are a conscience-ridden race, with a strong sense of the sinfulness of poverty. One cannot imagine the average Englishman deliberately turning parasite, and this national character does not necessarily change because a man is thrown out of work. Indeed, if one remembers that a tramp is only an Englishman out of work, forced by law to live as a vagabond, then the tramp-monster vanishes. I am not saying, of course, that most tramps are ideal characters; I am only saying that they are ordinary human beings, and that if they are worse than other people it is the result and not the cause of their way of life.

Text Passage: Father had already spoken to old Grimmett, the grocer, who wanted a smart lad and was willing to take me into the shop immediately. Meanwhile Father was going to get rid of the errand boy, and Joe was to come home and help with the shop till he got a regular job. Joe had left school some time back and had been more or less loafing ever since. Father had sometimes talked of 'getting him into' the accounts department at the brewery, and earlier had even had thoughts of making him into an auctioneer. Both were completely hopeless because Joe, at seventeen, wrote a hand like a ploughboy and couldn't repeat the multiplication table. At present he was supposed to be 'learning the trade' at a big bicycle shop on the outskirts of Walton. Tinkering with bicycles suited Joe, who, like most half-wits, had a slight mechanical turn, but he was quite incapable of working steadily and spent all his time loafing about in greasy overalls, smoking Woodbines, getting into fights, drinking (he's started that already), getting 'talked of' with one girl after another, and sticking Father for money. Father was worried, puzzled, and vaguely resentful. I can see him yet, with the meal on his bald head, and the bit of grey hair over his ears, and his spectacles and his grey moustache. He couldn't understand what was happening to him. For years his profits had gone up, slowly and steadily, ÃÂÃÂ£10 this year, ÃÂÃÂ£20 that year, and now suddenly they'd gone down with a bump. He couldn't understand it. He'd inherited the business from his father, he'd done an honest trade, worked hard, sold sound goods, swindled nobodyÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂand his profits were going down. He said a number of times, between sucking at his teeth to get the crumb out, that times were very bad, trade seemed very slack, he couldn't think what had come over people, it wasn't as if the horses didn't have to eat. Perhaps it was these here motors, he decided finally. 'Nasty smelly things!' Mother put in. She was a little worried, and knew that she ought to be more so. Once or twice while Father was talking there was a far-away look in her eyes and I could see her lips moving. She was trying to decide whether it should be a round of beef and carrots tomorrow or another leg of mutton. Except when there was something in her own line that needed foresight, such as buying linen or saucepans, she wasn't really capable of thinking beyond tomorrow's meals. The shop was giving trouble and Father was worriedÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂthat was about as far as she saw into it. None of us had any grasp of what was happening. Father had had a bad year and lost money, but was he really frightened by the future? I don't think so. This was 1909, remember. He didn't know what was happening to him, he wasn't capable of foreseeing that these Sarazin people would systematically under-sell him, ruin him, and eat him up. How could he? Things hadn't happened like that when he was a young man. All he knew was that times were bad, trade was very 'slack', very 'slow' (he kept repeating these phrases), but probably things would 'look up presently'.

Text Passage: The others had some hooks and lines and floats and a lump of bread paste in a rag, and we all cut ourselves willow switches from the tree at the corner of the pool. The farmhouse was only about two hundred yards away, and you had to keep out of sight because old Brewer was very down on fishing. Not that it made any difference to him, he only used the pool for watering his cattle, but he hated boys. The others were still jealous of me and kept telling me to get out of the light and reminding me that I was only a kid and knew nothing about fishing. They said that I was making such a noise I'd scare all the fish away, though actually I was making about half as much noise as anyone else there. Finally they wouldn't let me sit beside them and sent me to another part of the pool where the water was shallower and there wasn't so much shade. They said a kid like me was sure to keep splashing the water and frighten the fish away. It was a rotten part of the pool, a part where no fish would ordinarily come. I knew that. I seemed to know by a kind of instinct the places where a fish would lie. Still, I was fishing at last. I was sitting on the grass bank with the rod in my hands, with the flies buzzing round, and the smell of wild peppermint fit to knock you down, watching the red float on the green water, and I was happy as a tinker although the tear-marks mixed up with dirt were still all over my face.

He loses his memory in the hospital and all. He comes out of the hospital and doesn't know who the hell he is. He's really a duke, but he doesn't know it. Then he meets this nice, homey, sincere girl. They start talking about Charles Dickens. He's their favorite author and all. He's carrying this copy of Oliver Twist and so is she. I could've puked. Anyway, they fell in love right away, because they're both so nuts about Charles Dickens and all, and he helps her run her publishing business. She's a publisher, the girl. Only, her business isn't so good, because her brother's a drunkard and he spends all their money. Her brother was a doctor in the war and now he can't operate any more because his nerves are shot, so he drinks all the time, but he's pretty witty and all. Anyway, old Alec writes a book, and this girl publishes it, and they both make a lot of money on it. They're going to get married when this other girl, old Marcia, Alec's fiancee before he lost his memory, recognizes him when he's in this bookshop autographing books. She tells old Alec he's really a duke and all, but he doesn't believe her and doesn't want to go with her to visit his mother who is blind as a bat and all. But the other girl, the publisher, makes him go. She's very noble and all. So he goes. But he still doesn't get his memory back, even when his great Dane jumps all over him. Then, one day, some kids are playing cricket on the lawn and he gets smacked in the head with a cricket ball. Then right away he gets his goddam memory back and he goes in and kisses his mother on the forehead and all. Then he starts being a duke again, and he forgets all about the girl that has the publishing business. I won't tell you the rest of the story because I might puke if I did. Anyway, in the end, Alec and the publisher get married, and her drunkard brother gets his nerves back and operates on Alec's mother so she can see again, and then the drunken brother and old Marcia fall in love. At the end of the movie they all are sitting at this long dinner table laughing their asses off because the great Dane comes in with a bunch of puppies. Everybody thought that it was a male, I think, or some goddam thing. All I can say is, don't see it if you don't want to puke all over yourself.

He turned back to the window and the view of the school roof and put his cigar into his mouth againÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂbut at once took it out. "Damn him, anyway," he said. He turned around, looking both tense and agitated, and pulled out the straight chair at his mother's writing table and sat down. Text Passage: this on is something that happened to me at the local supermarket today. (No new paragraph. I'll spare you that.) I was standing at the meat counter, waiting for some rib lamb chops to be cut. A young mother and her little girl were waiting around, too. The little girl was about four, and, to pass the time, she leaned her back against the glass showcase and stared up at my unshaven face. I told her she was about the prettiest little girl I'd seen all day. Which made sense to her; she nodded. I said I'd bet she had a lot of boy friends. I got the same nod again. I asked her how many boy friends she had. She held up two fingers. "Two!" I said. "That's a lot of boy friends. What are their names, sweetheart?" Said she, in a piercing voice, "Bobby and Dorothy." I grabbed my lamb chops and ran. But that's exactly what brought on this letterÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂmuch more than Bessie's insistence that I write to you about Ph.D.s and acting. That, and a haiku-style poem I found in the hotel room where Seymour shot himself. It was written in pencil on the desk blotter: "The little girl on the plane/ Who turned her doll's head around/ To look at me." With these two things on my mind, I thought as I was driving home from the supermarket that at long last I could write to you and tell you why S. and I took over your and Franny's education as early and as highhandedly as we did. We've never put it into words for you, and I think it's high time one of us did. But now I'm not so sure I can do it. The little girl at the meat counter is gone, and I can't quite see the polite face of the little doll on the plane. And the old horror of being a professional writer, and the usual stench of words that goes with it, is beginning to drive me out of my seat. It seems terribly important to try, though. The age differences in the family always seemed to add unnecessarily and perversely to our problems. Not really between S. and the twins and Boo Boo and me, but between the two twosomes of you and Franny and S. and me. Seymour and I were both adultsÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂhe was even long out of collegeÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂby the time you and Franny were both able to read. At that stage, we had no real urge even to push our favorite classics at the two of youÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂnot, anyway, with the same gusto that we had at the twins or Boo Boo. We knew there's no keeping a born scholar ignorant, and at heart, I think, we didn't really want to, but we were nervous, even frightened, at the statistics on child pedants and academic weisenheimers who grow up into faculty-recreation-room savants. For one reason, he was not really short-nosed. For another, cigars, with Zooey, were not in any patent way a young man's affectation. He had been smoking them since he was sixteen, and regularly, as many as a dozen a day ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂexpensive panatelas, for the most partÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂsince he was eighteen. A Vermont-marble coffee table, rectangular and quite long, stood parallel and very close to the couch. Zooey abruptly went over to it. She raised up on one arm, and said, "Whew." She squinted at the morning sunlight. "Why's it so sunny?" She only partly took in Zooey's presence. "Why's it so sunny?" she repeated. Zooey observed her rather narrowly. "I bring the sun wherever I go, buddy," he said. Franny, still squinting, stared at him. "Why'd you wake me up?" she asked. She was still too heavy with sleep to sound really fractious, but it was apparent that she felt there was some kind of injustice in the air. "Well . . . it's like this. Effortlessly, by softening and thinning his voice, rather than by raising it to a falsetto, he gave what was to Franny a familiar and always realistic imitation of their mother passing along a few cautionary words: "We say many things in heat, young lady, that we don't really mean and are very sorry for the next day." Then, instantly, he frowned, opened his eyes, and stared for several seconds at the ceiling. "Firstly," he said, "I think you think I have intentions of trying to take your prayer away from you or something. I don't. I do not. You can lie on that couch reciting the preamble to the Constitution for the rest of your life, as far as I'm concerned, but what I am tryingÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ" "That's a beautiful start. Just beautitul." "Beg pardon?" "Oh, shut up. Just go on, go on." "What I started to say, I have nothing against the prayer at all. No matter what you think. You're not the first one who ever thought of saying it, you know. I once went to every Army & Navy store in New York looking for a nice, pilgrim-type rucksack. I was going to fill it with bread crumbs and start walking all over the goddam country. Saying the prayer. Spreading the Word. The whole business." Zooey hesitated. "And I don't just mention it, for God's sake, to show you I was once an Emotional Young Person Just Like Yourself." "Why do you mention it, then?" "Why do I mention it? I mention it because I have a couple of things I want to say to you, and it's just possible I'm not qualified to say them. On the ground that I once had a strong desire to say the prayer myself but didn't. For all I know, I may be a little jealous of your having a go at it. It's very possible, in fact. In the first place, I'm a ham. It may very well be that I hate like hell to play Martha to somebody else's Mary. Who the hell knows?" Franny didn't choose to reply. But she drew Bloomberg slightly closer to her and gave him an odd, ambiguous little hug. Then she looked over in her brother's direction, and said, "You're a brownie. Did you know that?" Text Passage: I've just finished decoding a long letter that came from Mother this morning, all about you and General Eisenhower's smile and small boys in the Daily News who fall down elevator shafts and when am I going to have my phone in New York taken out and get one installed up here in the country, where I really need it. Surely the only woman in the world who can write a letter in invisible italics. Dear Bessie. I get five hundred words of copy from her like clockwork every three months on the subject of my poor old private phone and how stupid it is to pay Good Money every month for something nobody's ever even around to use any more. Which is really a big fat lie. When I'm in town, I invariably sit talking by the hour with my old friend Yama, the God of Death, and a private phone's a must for our little chats. Anyway, please tell her I haven't changed my mind. I love that old phone with a passion. It was the only really private property Seymour and I ever had in Bessie's entire kibbutz. It's also essential to my inner harmony to see Seymour's listing in the goddam phone book every year. I like to browse through the G's confidently. Be a good boy and pass that message along for me. Not quite word for word, but nicely. Be kinder to Bessie, Zooey, when you can. I don't think I mean because she's our mother, but because she's weary. You will after you're thirty or so, when everybody slows down a little (even you, maybe), but try harder now. It isn't enough to treat her with the doting brutality of an apache dancer toward his partnerÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂwhich she understands, incidentally, whether you think so or not. You forget that she thrives on sentimentality almost as much as Les does. My telephone problems aside, Bessie's current letter is really a Zooey letter. I'm to write and tell you that you have your Whole Life Before You and that it's Criminal if you don't go after your Ph.D. before you go in for the actor's life in a big way. She doesn't say what she'd like you to get the Ph.D. in, but I assume Math rather than Greek, you dirty little bookworm. At any rate, I gather that she wants you to have something to Fall Back On if for some reason the acting career doesn't work out. Which may be very sound, and probably is, but I don't feel like coming right out and saying so. The second-eldest child, Buddy, was what is 'known in campus-catalogue parlance as "writer-in-residence" at a girls' junior college in upper New York State. He lived alone, in a small, unwinterized, unelectrified house about a quarter of a mile away from a rather popular ski-run. The next-eldest of the children, Boo Boo, was married and the mother of three children. In November, 1955, she was travelling in Europe with her husband and all three of their children. In order of age, the twins, Walt and Waker, come after Boo Boo. Walt had been dead just over ten years. He was killed in a freakish explosion while he was with the Army of Occupation in Japan. Waker, his junior by some twelve minutes, was a Roman Catholic priest, and in November, 1955, he was in Ecuador, attending a Jesuit conference of some kind. Public response to the children was often hot and never tepid. In general, listeners were divided into two, curiously restive camps: those who held that the Glasses were a bunch of insufferably "superior" little bastards that should have been drowned or gassed at birth, and those who held that they were bona-fide underage wits and savants, of an uncommon, if unenviable, order. At this writing (1957), there are former listeners to "It's a Wise Child" who remember, with basically astonishing accuracy, many of the individual performances of each of the seven children. In this same thinning but still oddly coterielike group, the consensus is that, of all the Glass children, the eldest boy, Seymour, back in the late twenties and early thirties, had been the "best" to hear, the most consistently "rewarding." After Seymour, Zooey, the youngest boy in the family, is generally placed second in order of preference, or appeal. And since we have a singularly workaday interest in Zooey here, it may be appended that, as an ex-panelist on "It's a Wise Child," he had one almanaclike distinction among (or over) his brothers and sisters. Off and on, during their broadcasting years, all seven of the children had been fair game for the kind of child psychologist or professional educator who takes a special interest in extra-precocious children. Text Passage: It was Monday and all, and pretty near Christmas, and all the stores were open. So it wasn't too bad walking on Fifth Avenue. All those Santa Clauses were standing on corners ringing those bells. It was pretty Christmasy all of a sudden. A million little kids were there with their mothers, getting on and off buses and coming in and out of stores. I walked and walked up Fifth Avenue. Then all of a sudden, something very spooky started happening. Every time when I started to cross the street, I had this feeling that I would never get to the other side of the street. I thought I would just go down, down, down, and nobody would ever see me again. You can't imagine how it scared me. Then I started doing something else. Every time when I started to cross the street, I imagined that I was saying to my brother Allie, "Allie, don't let me disappear. Allie, don't let me disappear. Allie, don't let me disappear. Please, Allie." And then, when I was on the other side of the street without disappearing, I thanked him. I walked and walked. I was sort of afraid to stop, I think - I don't remember, to tell you the truth. But finally, I stopped and sat down on this bench. I sat there, I think, for about an hour. Finally, I decided that I would go away and never go home again and I would never go away to another school again. I decided to see old Phoebe and sort of say good-by to her and all, and give her back her Christmas dough, and then start hitchhiking my way out West where it was very pretty and sunny and where nobody would know me and I would get a job. I could get a job at a filling station somewhere, putting gas and oil in people's cars. I thought I would pretend that I was one of those deaf-mutes. That way there would be no goddam stupid useless conversations with anybody. If anybody wanted to tell me something, they would have to write it on a piece of paper and show it to me. They would get bored as hell doing that after a while, and then there would be no conversations for the rest of my life. I would build me a little cabin somewhere and live there for the rest of my life. I would build it near the woods, but not in the woods, because I want a sunny as hell place all the time. And later on, if I wanted to get married or something, I would meet this beautiful girl, also a deaf-mute, and we'd get married. We would live in my cabin, and if she wanted to say anything to me, she'd have to write it on a goddam piece of paper, as everybody else. If we had any children, we would hide them somewhere. We could buy them a lot of books and teach them how to read and write by ourselves.

She was still stroking Bloomberg, still succoring him, forcibly, into the subtle and difficult world outside warm afghans. "They look starved," Zooey said, but withdrew his hand from the fish food. Text Passage: I walked all the way back to the hotel because I didn't want to take another stinking cab. There was almost no snow on the sidewalks. But it was very cold, and I took my red hunting hat out of my pocket and put it on. I wished I knew who had stolen my gloves at Pencey, because my hands were freezing. Even if I had known, I would not have done much about it. I'm one of these very yellow guys. I try not to show it, but I am. For example, if I had known who had stolen my gloves, I probably would have gone down to the crook's room and said, "Okay. How about giving those gloves back to me?" Then the crook that had stolen them probably would have said, "What gloves?" Then I probably would have gone in his closet and found the gloves somewhere. I would have taken them out and showed them to the guy and said, "These are your goddam gloves?" Then the crook probably would have said, "I never saw those gloves before in my life. If they're yours, take them. I don't want the goddam things." I would feel that I ought to hit the guy in the jaw or something - break his goddam jaw. Only, I wouldn't have the guts to do it. I might say something very snotty instead of hitting him in the jaw. Then he would probably say, "Listen, Caulfield. Are you calling me a crook?" Then, instead of saying, "Yes, you're a crook!" I probably would say, "All I know is my goddam gloves were in your goddam galoshes." Right away then, the guy would know for sure that I wasn't going to hit him, and he probably would say, "Are you calling me a thief?" Then I probably would say, "Nobody's calling anybody a thief. All I know is my gloves were in your goddam galoshes." Finally, I would leave his room without hitting him. It's no fun to be yellow. Maybe I'm not all yellow. I don't know. I think maybe I'm just partly yellow and partly the guy that doesn't feel sorry very much if he loses his gloves. Some guys spend days looking for something they lost. One of my troubles is, I never care too much when I lose something. Maybe that's why I'm partly yellow. It's no excuse, though. What you should be is not yellow at all. If you sort of feel that you ought to hit somebody in the jaw, you should do it. I'm just no good at it, though. I hate fist fights.

The night table that ordinarily stood alongside the bed had been moved close enough to it so that Franny could reach it without quite standing up. She put her hand under a particularly soiled-looking piece of canvas covering it and passed the hand back and forth till she found what she was looking forÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂa porcelain cigarette box and a box of matches in a copper holder. She lit a cigarette, then gave the phone another, long, exceedingly worried look. With the exception of her late brother Seymour, it should be noted, all her brothers had overly vibrant, not to say sinewy, voices on the telephone. At this hour, it was very possible that Franny felt deeply hesitant about taking a chance on just the timbre, let alone the verbal content, of any of her brothers' voices on the phone. However, she puffed nervously on her cigarette and, rather bravely, picked up the phone. "Hello. Buddy?" she said. "Hello, sweetheart. How are youÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂare you all right?" "I'm fine. How are you? You sound as though you have a cold." Then, when there was no immediate response: "I suppose Bessie's been briefing you by the hour." "WellÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂafter a fashion. Yes and no. You know. Are you all right, sweetheart?" "I'm fine. You sound funny, though. Either you have a terrible cold or this is a terrible connection. Where are you, anyway?" "Where am I? I'm right in my element, Flop-sy. I'm in a little haunted house down the road. Never mind. Just talk to me." Franny unplacidly crossed her legs. "I don't know exactly what you'd like to talk about," she said. "What all'd Bessie tell you, I mean?" There was a most characteristically Buddy-like pause at the other end. It was exactly the kind of pauseÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂjust a trifle rich with seniority of yearsÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂthat had often tried the patience of both Franny and the vif tuoso at the other end of the phone when they were small children. "Well, I'm not terribly sure what all she told me, sweetheart. Past a certain point, it's a little rude to go on listening to Bessie on the phone. I heard about the cheeseburger diet, you can be sure. And, of course, the Pilgrim books. Then I think I just sat with the phone at my ear, not really listening. You know." "Oh," Franny said. She switched her cigarette over to her telephone hand and, with her free hand, reached again under the canvas cover on the night table and found a tiny ceramic ashtray, which she placed beside her on the bed. "You sound funny," she said. "Do you have a cold, or what?" "I feel wonderful, sweetheart. I'm sitting here talking to you and I feel wonderful. It's a joy to hear your voice. I can't tell you." Franny once again pushed back her hair with one hand. She didn't say anything. "Flopsy? Can you think of anything Bessie may have missed? You feel like talking at all?" With her fingers, Franny slightly altered the position of the tiny ashtray beside her on the bed. "Well," she said, "I'm a little talked out, to be honest with you. Zooey's been at me all morning."

Text Passage: At the end of the first act we went out with all the other jerks for a cigarette. What a deal that was. You never saw so many phonies in all your life. Everybody was smoking their ears off and talking about the play so that everybody could hear and know how sharp they were. Some stupid movie actor was standing near us, having a cigarette. I don't know his name, but he always plays the part of a guy in a war movie that gets yellow before it's time to go over the top. He was with some beautiful blonde, and the two of them were trying to look as if he didn't even know that people were looking at him. Modest as hell. I got a big bang out of it. Old Sally didn't talk much, except to rave about the Lunts. Then all of a sudden, she saw some jerk on the other side of the lobby. Some guy very well dressed. Strictly Ivy League. Big deal. He was standing next to the wall, smoking himself to death and looking bored as hell. Old Sally said several times, "I know that boy from somewhere." I got bored as hell, and I said to her, "Why don't you go on over and give him a big kiss, if you know him? He'll enjoy it." She got sore when I said that. Finally, the jerk noticed her and came over and said hello. Old Sally introduced us. It was funny when old Sally asked him how he liked the play. He was the kind of a phony that have to give themselves room when they answer somebody's question. He stepped back, and stepped right on the lady's foot behind him. He probably broke every toe in her body. He said the play itself was no masterpiece, but that the Lunts, of course, were absolute angels. Angels. For Chrissake. Angels. That killed me. Then he and old Sally started talking about a lot of people they both knew. It was the phoniest conversation you ever heard in your life. When the next act was over, they continued their goddam boring conversation. I even thought for a minute that he was going to get in the goddam cab with us when the show was over, because he walked about two blocks with us, but he had to meet a bunch of phonies for cocktails, he said. I could see them all sitting around in some bar, criticizing shows and books and women in those tired, snobby voices. They kill me, those guys.

Text Passage: Mrs. Glass, still staring at him, let him pass. Then, almost at once, she made for the living room, at a clip that scarcely gave her leave to call back over her shoulder, "Change that shirt, young man!" If Zooey heard this, he gave no sign. At the far end of the hall, he went into the bedroom he had once shared with his twin brothers, which now, in 1955, was his alone. But he stayed in his room for not more than two minutes. When he came out, he had on the same sweaty shirt. There was, however, a slight but fairly distinct change in his appearance. He had acquired a cigar, and lighted it. And for some reason he had an unfolded white handkerchief draped over his head, possibly to ward off rain, or hail, or brimstone. He went directly across the hall and into the room his two eldest brothers had shared. This was the first time in almost seven years that Zooey had, in the ready-made dramatic idiom, "set foot" in Seymour's and Buddy's old room. Discounting a totally negligible incident a couple of years earlier, when he had methodically dragged the entire apartment for a mislaid or "stolen" tennis-racket press. He closed the door behind him as tightly as possible, and with an expression implying that the absence of a key in the lock met with his disapproval. He gave the room itself scarcely a glance, once he was inside it. Instead, he turned around and deliberately faced a sheet of what had once been snow-white beaverboard that was nailed uncompromisingly to the back of the door. It was a mammoth specimen, very nearly as long and as wide as the door itself. One could have believed that its whiteness, smoothness, and expanse had at one time cried out rather plaintively for India ink and block lettering. Certainly not in vain, if so. Every inch of visible surface of the board had been decorated, with four somewhat gorgeous-looking columns of quotations from a variety of the world's literatures. The lettering was minute, but jet-black and passionately legible, if just a trifle fancy in spots, and without blots or erasures. The workmanship was no less fastidious even at the bottom of the board, near the doorsill, where the two penmen, each in his turn, had obviously lain on their stomachs. No attempt whatever had been made to assign quotations or authors to categories or groups of any kind. So that to read the quotations from top to bottom, column by column, was rather like walking through an emergency station set up in a flood area, where, for example, Pascal had been unribaldly bedded down with Emily Dickinson, and where, so to speak, Baudelaire's and Thomas a Kempis's toothbrushes were hanging side by side. Zooey, standing in just close enough, read the top entry in the left-hand column, then went on reading downward. From his expression, or lack of it, he might have been killing time on a railway platform reading a billboard advertisement for Dr. Scholl's foot pads.

Text Passage: THE last, the under, page of the four-year-old letter was stained a sort of off-cordovan color, and it was torn in two places along the folds. Zooey, finished reading, treated it with some little care as he put the letter back into page-one order. He tapped the pages, to even them out, against his dry knees. He frowned. Then, mercurially, as though he'd read the letter, by God, for the last time in his life, he stuffed it like so much excelsior into its envelope. He placed the thick envelope on the side of the tub and began to play a little game with it. With one finger he tapped the loaded envelope back and forth along the tub edge, seeing, apparently, if he could keep it in motion without letting it fall into the tub water. After a good five minutes of this, he gave the envelope a faulty tap and had to reach out quickly and grab it. Which ended the game. Keeping the retrieved envelope in his hand, he sat lower, deeper, in the water, letting his knees submerge. He stared abstractedly for a minute or two at the tiled wall beyond the foot of the tub, then glanced at his cigarette on the soapcatch, picked it off, and took a couple of test drags on it, but it had gone out. He sat up again, very abruptly, with a great slosh of tub water, and dropped his dry left hand over the side of the tub. A typewritten manuscript was lying, face up, on the bathmat. He picked it up and brought it aboard, as it were. He stared at it briefly, then inserted his four-year-old letter in the middle pages, where the stapling in a manuscript is tightest. He then propped the manuscript against his now wet knees, an inch or so above the waterline, and began to turn the pages. When he came to page 9, he folded the manuscript, magazine-style, and began to read or to study. The role of "Rick" had been heavily underlined with a soft-lead pencil. TINA (morosely): Oh, darling, darling, darling. I'm not much good to you, am I? RICK: Don't say that. Don't ever say that, you hear me? TINA: It's true, though. I'm a jinx. I'm a horrible jinx. If it hadn't been for me, Scott Kincaid would have assigned you to the Buenos Aires office ages ago. I spoiled all that.

Text Passage: I still had to get those damn theater tickets. So I went and bought two tickets for I Know My Love. I didn't much want to see it, but I knew that old Sally, the queen of the phonies, would be beyond herself with joy when I told her that I had tickets for that, because the famous actor and actress, the Lunts, were in it and all. She liked such shows, with famous actors. I don't. I don't like any shows very much, if you want to know the truth. They're not as bad as movies, but they're certainly nothing to rave about. In the first place, I hate actors. They never act like people. They just think that they do. And if any actor's really good, you can always see that he knows that he's good, and that spoils it. You take Sir Laurence Olivier, for example. I saw him in Hamlet, D.B. took Phoebe and me to see it last year. He'd already seen it, and he spoke about it at lunch so well that I was anxious as hell to see it, too. But I didn't enjoy it much. I just don't see what's so wonderful about Sir Laurence Olivier, that's all. He has a terrific voice, and he's a helluva handsome guy, and he's very nice when he's walking or dueling or something, but he wasn't at all Hamlet. He was too much like a goddam general, instead of a sad, screwed-up type guy. The best part in the whole show was when old Ophelia's brother - the one that gets in the duel with Hamlet at the very end - was going away and his father was giving him a lot of advice. While the father was giving him a lot of advice, old Ophelia was sort of horsing around with her brother, taking his dagger out of the holster, and teasing him and all while he was trying to look interested in the bull his father was shooting. I think I must read that play by myself. The trouble with me is, I always have to read that stuff by myself. It was the first one we did on filmÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂI don't think you saw it, you were at school or something. I played a young farmer in it who lives all alone with his father. The boy has a notion that he hates farming, and he and his father have always had a terrible time making a living, so when the father dies, he sells all the cattle and makes big plans to go to the big city to make a living," Zooey picked up the snowman again but didn't give it a shake-merely turned it around, by the pedestal. "It had some nice bits," he said. "After I sell all the cows, I keep going out to the pasture to look for them. And when I go for a farewell walk with my girl, right before I leave for the big city, I keep steering her over toward the empty pasture. Then, when I get to the big city and get a job, I spend all my spare time hanging around the stockyards. Finally, in heavy traffic on the main street in the big city, a car makes a left turn and changes into a cow. I run after it, just as the light changes, and get run overÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂstampeded." He gave the snowman a shake. "It probably wasn't anything you couldn't watch while you were cutting your toenails, but at least you didn't feel like slinking home from the studio after rehearsals. I'm sick to death of being the heavy in everybody's life. God, you should see Hess and LeSage when they're talking about a new show. Or a new anything. They're as happy as pigs till I show up. I feel like those dismal bastards Seymour's beloved Chuang-tzu warned everybody against. 'Beware when the socalled sagely men come limping into sight.'" He sat still, watching the snowflakes swirl. "I could happily lie down and die sometimes," he said. Franny at that moment was gazing at a sunlit faded spot in the carpet over near the piano, her lips very discernibly moving. "This is all so funny, you can't imagine," she said, with the faintest tremor in her voice, and Zooey looked over at her. Her paleness was emphasized by the fact that she was wearing no lipstick at all. Text Passage: She shuddered. "It was just horrible. So spidery. I've never had such a spidery nightmare in my entire life." "Spiders, eh? That's very interesting. Very significant. I had a very interesting case in Zurich, some years backÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂa young person very much like yourself, as a matter of factÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ" "Be quiet a second, or I'll forget it," Franny said. She stared avidly into space, as nightmare-recallers do. There were half circles under her eyes, and other, subtler signs that mark an acutely troubled young girl, but nonetheless no one could have missed seeing that she was a first-class beauty. Her skin was lovely, and her features were delicate and most distinctive. Her eyes were very nearly the same quite astonishing shade of blue as Zooey's, but were set farther apart, as a sister's eyes no doubt should beÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂand they were not, so to speak, a day's work to look into, as Zooey's were. Some four years earlier, at her graduation from boarding school, her brother Buddy had morbidly prophesied to himself, as she grinned at him from the graduates' platform, that she would in all probability one day marry a man with a hacking cough. So there was that in her face, too. "Oh, God, I remember it now!" she said. "It was just hideous. I was at a swimming pool somewhere, and a whole bunch of people kept making me dive for a can of Medaglia d'Oro coffee that was on the bottom. Every time I'd come up, they'd make me go down again. I was crying, and I kept saying to everybody, 'You have your bathing suits on. Why don't you do a little diving, too?,' but they'd all just laugh and make these terribly snide little remarks, and down I'd go again." She gave another shudder. "These two girls that are in my dorm were there. Stephanie Logan, and a girl I hardly even knowÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂsomebody, as a matter of fact, I always felt terribly sorry for, because she had such an awful name. Shannon Sherman. They both had a big oar, and they kept trying to hit me with it every time I'd surface." Franny put her hands over her eyes briefly. "Whew!" She shook her head. She reflected. "The only person that made any sense in the dream was Professor Tupper. I mean he was the only person that was there that I know really detests me." "Detests you, eh? Very interesting." Zooey's cigar was in his mouth. He revolved it slowly between his fingers, like a dream-interpreter who isn't getting all the facts in the case. He looked very contented. "Why does he detest you?" he asked. "Without absolute frankness, you realize, my hands areÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ" "He detests me because I'm in this crazy Religion seminar he conducts, and I can never bring myself to smile back at him when he's being charming and Oxfordish. He's on lend-lease or something from Oxford, and he's just a terribly sad old self-satisfied phony with wild and woolly white hair. I think he goes into the men's room and musses it up before he conies to classÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂI honestly do. He has no enthusiasm whatever for his subject. Ego, yes. Enthusiasm, no. Which would be all rightÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂI mean it wouldn't be anything exactly strangeÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂbut he keeps dropping idiotic hints that he's a Realized Man himself and we should be pretty happy kids to have him in this country." Franny grimaced. "The only thing he does with any zing, when he isn't bragging, is correct somebody when they say something's Sanskrit when it's really Pali. He just knows I can't stand him! You should see the faces I make at him when he isn't looking." "What was he doing at the pool?"

At the forefront rode the figure of the old man, his eyes squinting against the rising sun, face a leather map of life's bruises, a hat pulled low to fend off the stubborn insistence of the day. Beneath the unravaging sky, the spare landscape spread out in merciless serenity. Beside him, a younger man marked by the brash impetuosity of youth held the leather reins taut, his gaze fixed on some invisible promontory where old wrongs might be righted or at least remembered anew. The sun stained the horizon red and gold, a cracked eggshell bleeding, but the riders paid it no heed, driven by causes that lay buried deeper than roots of mesquite trees twisted in their eternal grasp for anything that would sustain them. They rode on, ensconced in the silence wordless and complete like a room long abandoned. Their shadows stretched thin over a land that would forget them soon enough, but for now, those shadows rode alongside as though acknowledging the harmony of man and beast in one lonely pilgrimage toward whatever reckoning lay at trail's end. The old man turned slightly to appraise his surroundings, acutely aware of the vastness of the land and the smallness of the saddle between his legs, the rawhide creak beneath him a counterpoint to the whisper of a confession he knew he'd never make. He felt the pull of history in his bones, a weight older than time, and as the remnants of their dust-cloud settled, he eased up on the reins, briefly lifting his weathered face to the heavens as if beseeching the gods for nothing more nor less than the continuation of his own course, which he knew as sure as the earth beneath him was unlikely to alter in its orbit for any prayers uttered or debts paid.

Text Passage: Dust hung in the air like some ghostly specter, settling silent upon the old cabin where the man stood, hands resting on a rusted rifle, eyes sunken deep into his skull. The sun slipped toward the horizon, a blood-red eye closing over a desolate earth. He looked down where the road vanished into deep woods gone grey with shadow, and he thought of the boy, thin and frail, somewhere in that murky dark, legs moving through the underbrush, fear in his hollow bones. The man took a breath, a slow shuddering thing that rattled his ribs and echoed in his chest. He could feel the end like the distant murmur of wolves, a low note thrumming through his marrow. The world felt long dead but he was not yet, and the boy was not yet, and therein lay the cruel tendril of hope. He stepped out from the crumbling porch, a specter himself, merging with the night's deepening shade, becoming form and void alike, his footsteps silent upon the earth that seemed to recoil at the touch of life. Darkness ate him, swallowed him whole. The trees, skeletal and vast, loomed around him, their branches scribing unknown tongues against the bruised sky above. He thought maybe they whispered, their language lost to any but the mad, and he thought that perhaps he owned the right kind of brokenness to understand. The cabin was long gone behind him, only distance and shadowing ahead, and somewhere the boy, a lone creature adrift in a wilderness of forgotten things. The man moved like a whisper, carrying with him the smell of smoke and copper and all the memories that world would not allow him to abandon. Each step felt heavier than the last, weighed by the burden of roads not taken, of those he could not save. His fingers tightened on the rifle, its steel cold and comforting in the absence of warmth found elsewhere. Night engulfed him, pressing closer, yet a part of him embraced it, felt at home within its formless recesses. He stopped, head turning to catch the faintest trace of movement, the brushed sound like a critter through the fallen leaves. But no, it was nothing, the silence a vast thing pressing upon his ears with the weight of truth spoken and unspoken. The man pushed on, the trees solid and silent arbiters of his journey, their ranks endless and unyielding. And he knew, with the certainty that marked truth from lie, that the boy needed him, that hope and despair held hands in the dark forest, carving paths through shadow and silence. The rifle felt lighter now, a companion rather than a burden, and the man allowed himself the ghost of a smile, bitter and sharp against his worn skin, as he pressed on through the world that would consume him without ceremony, without mourning.

Text Passage: In the still achromatic dawn, a lean figure trudged across the desolate plain, the coarse grit of a nearly forgotten world crunching beneath his boots. Shadows stretched long and thin, like the fingers of some unseen specter reaching out from the nether, beckoning the traveler tither, here in a land as withered as a biblical desert. Sparse mesas jutted from the earth like the hulking bones of some ancient cataclysm, their surfaces pockmarked by the interminable strife of sun and wind. There was no breeze now, only the oppressive silence that settled over the landscape like a shroud, broken occasionally by the distant lament of a solitary raven circling in the washed-out sky. His eyes, dark as bitumen and fathomless as old wells, scanned the horizon with a weary knowing, the burden of centuries seated in the slope of his shoulders. Beneath his frayed coat, he bore the weight of a revolver, its grip slick with the patina of old leather and sweat, a tacit safeguard against the lurking inevitabilities of this forsaken land. The path wound serpentine-like in front of him, offering no guidance, demanding obeisance to whatever stygian compass lay rooted in the veined earth. The man regarded it with indifference, the map of his journey etched in scars across his memory, the pale ghosts of long-buried fears threading an incomplete story in the recesses of his mind. Toward the west, the languorous sun climbed with grudging reluctance, casting copper lines of light that sheared the crests of the broken desert, revealing the terrible beauty of solitude in its purest form. The land, old as time yet unyielding in its simplicity, held no promise of redemption save in its raw endurance. Somewhere, far beyond reckon, a dim parish bell tolled its solitary note, a grim reminder of endurance and the silence it commands. He continued onward, the rhythm of his footsteps a metronome marking unfathomable distances, the imperfect motif of time eroded, leaving nothing but the purgation of repetition. They rose, the man and the boy, from the shelter of their rough-hewn sanctuary that the night had so grudgingly embraced. The fire long dead, cinders swallowed by frost, leaving the air with a taste of charred hopes and bygone warmth. He strapped the few possessions they owned back onto the cart, its wheels tired from the burden of stoic endurance, and they set forth along the road that meandered like a thought half-formed. Their journey lay ahead, unrelenting, continued in the contours of their resolve woven like threadbare cloth. 

The land stretched around them in a desolate sprawl, a forsaken testament to the days where verdant fields once waxed fat under the sun's bounty. Now there was only the earth, bruised and barren, where once the color of life had flown as freely as the air. The sky, slate-gray and vast, hung above them as if waiting mutely for some revelation yet to come, cloaked with the heaviness of uncertainty. They walked, their footsteps a drumbeat, echoing an older, patient rhythm. 

Upon reaching a shallow dell, they paused. The boy pointed to a creature lying prostrate, bones wound tight in a shroud of skin. A lamb, or what was left of it, staring blindly at the heavens it had long ceased to comprehend. Its eyes reflecting the fragile insignificance of being. The man crouched, his fingers tracing the curve of its skull, cold and indifferent. He knew death in its myriad forms. He coaxed the boy onward, their shadows long against the pallid earth as the sun glared down with impotent ferocity. 

They pressed on, upwards toward the ridge where the bones of ancient trees clawed against the firmament. The man watched the boy beside him, the smallness of his form wrapped in the misfit quilt of ages lost. Each step deliberate as they marched south toward the heart of an unknown fate. They listened to the wind as it sobbed and danced across the skeletal branches, an unremembered tribute to the song of creation now stilled. 

By twilight, they stumbled upon a creek, water coiling aimlessly amongst stones washed smooth as fables from a forgotten time. The man crouched and cupped his hands, drinking deeply of the biting cold. He gestured for the boy to join him. They knelt together, a solemn sacrament shared in the presence of eternity. The boy shivered as they sat by the water's edge, the last light of the day kissing their faces with a softness that the world had long forsaken. In that fractured hour between day and night, he spoke to the boy of stars, of constellations forgotten, charioteers absent from the sky. The boy listened, his questions falling unasked, the answers already lost in the rhythms of the universe. As the shadows enveloped them, the man felt for the first time a tremor of the unknown that surged in the gathering darkness, held at bay only by the thread of hope they spun themselves upon.

On his back he bore a burlap sack filled with scarce belongings, dust lining the creases of his clothes, the hem of his pants shredded by thorns and rocks. Old Tom saw him first from where he sat mending the fence, his hat pushed up on his forehead, eyes squinting against the soft glow of the morning. He twisted a length of wire with the slow, deliberate motions of one who had worked all his life with his hands, eyes never leaving the figure that grew slowly, relentlessly, out of the dawn. When the man came into earshot, Tom stood, one hand resting on the handle of the tool he held, waiting. Text Passage: Lena had the clock turned face-down on the nightstand, as though the complicated business of its hands moving in a direction they frankly preferred, and had preferred since clocks learned to count, were too much to have gaping at her, and she kept discovering, with a kind of not entirely graceless horror, that the plain, innocent things in the room were full of opinions--her chipped blue mug with the lipstick crenellation said she ought to get out of bed, the little ficus she had talked into surviving January said she was impossible, really impossible, and the scarf she had draped over the bedside lamp, to make the bulb mind its manners, kept sliding down with an air that suggested it had better things to do--so when the phone on the floor hummed (a polite, beetle-minded hum, not the bold bellow of a phone that knows it's the hero of a life), she reached for it and didn't, and then did, and then didn't again, and it would have been very gratifying to tell the truth there and admit that she was above it all, that she was installed, with the seriousness of a small archduchess, in some difficult thought, but the fact was she had been counting the creases in her own palm just then, and had stopped at seventeen, which anyone could tell you is not even remotely a good stopping place; she looked instead at the postcards tacked half-heartedly to the window frame--one of a museum hallway where the light was behaving with such perfect decency you wanted to write it a thank-you note, one of a mountain that in person had been windy and indifferent--and thought she really ought to have better words pinned to her life, the way certain girls, whom she loved a little and resented almost as much, pinned ticket stubs and urgent sayings to cork boards and then got on with things as if you could be saved by an upholstery of reminders; she reached under the bedspread (which had acquired, overnight, a soft, greasy courage from the Chinese takeout she had sworn off forever twice last week) and patted for the matches, and when she found them, she lit a small, fussy candle that refused to be a ceremony and only managed being a flame, which is often all a ceremony is anyway; and she thought--she had to, it came the way the weather comes--that if her cousin Milo called (Milo with his instructive silences, which he seemed to have learned at a very modern school where they issue silences with narrow-ruled margins) she would tell him she was learning to breathe again, but not theatrically, not like people who speak about their lungs as if they were items they'd adopted and meant to return for something in a different color, and she might even bring up the pamphlet one of the smooth boys in the quad had handed her, with diagrams of atmospheres inside rib cages and instructions to be gentle with yourself written in a font that profoundly distrusted you; I get it. Really. There are days when the stairs to the subway feel not only steep but personally vindictive. There are days when the only honest thing in the entire city is the sour tang in a can of grapefruit soda, and even that betrays you by going flat mid-sip. But it is a very strange hobby, if you ask me, this business of making yourself the single honest measuring stick in a world of rubber rulers. You can't keep calling it some big roaring truth just because it roars in your own head; roars are cheap in apartments with thin walls. You said the kids in your seminar were doing that thing--your phrase, not mine--where they nod like dashboard dogs every time someone says "liminal," and you looked at me as if I were supposed to throw my drink at the wall in solidarity. I won't. I refuse to make even the smallest gesture that will require me to clean up after. The truth is, I once had a teacher who didn't so much teach as--how to put it--pour a very small, very steady stream of clear water into the dustiest corner of my skull, and if I'd been half as eager to pronounce the entire apparatus a circus back then as you are now, I would've missed it. You're allowed to dislike people. You're allowed to flinch from the particular sound of a particular laugh from a boy with an anemic mustache who says "problematic" like a ship's bell. But don't make a religion out of your flinching. And don't talk to me about purity as if it were a new product you found in a little shop that no one else has discovered. You are not a lighthouse, kid. You're a person with a very good ear for fakery, which is great so long as you don't start whispering that word at your own reflection. I'm not asking you to love anybody. I'm begging you not to hate everybody. There's a difference, and it's the difference between sleeping and pretending to sleep when Ma tiptoes in with that tragic saucer of sliced pears she thinks fixes everything. If you insist on combusting, at least do it at a safe distance from the curtains. And if you decide tomorrow to go back to class, I'll be the one on the fire escape with the stupid tin of almonds you like, not because almonds mean anything, but because it's something to put in your mouth besides the next terrible sentence you're dying to say about the way the world tilts.

Text Passage: It wasn't that I was in any condition to be impressed, if you want the ugly truth; I was sitting in my father's old bathrobe on the radiator with my knees going blotchy from the heat, listening to the mouthpiece breathe at me like it had the asthma, and the hall light was doing that pernicious yellow thing it does when the house is too clean and too quiet and the neighbors have finally stopped dropping shoes on their ceiling, which is our floor, and then this voice comes in--this ridiculous, careful, tweedy voice--saying he's Dr. Somebody from the university and he's very concerned about my "trajectory," and I swear to you I could hear the wick of the act before he even struck the match. Don't, I said. Just don't, Mona. You've got a whole department full of freshman boys to rehabilitate; leave my poor little trajectory to go where it's going, which is straight to the sink for a glass of tap water, after which it's going to lie down and dissolve. There was a pause--you know the kind that's half a performance in itself--and then she did the coughing bit, the polite professional cough, and I nearly choked laughing because she never could do anything halfway; it had to be the total production, with props and the right shoes and the whole Greco-Roman chorus if you let her. "You're not funny," I said, only I was already a little better from not letting her be anybody but herself. She said, Well, sweetness, maybe I'm not going for funny, maybe I'm going for effective, and anyway what do you want me to do, come over there and hold your hand while you scowl at me? And I said something cheap about how everybody in this family needed to sit on their hands for a decade or two and see if their mouths learned to shut without the bribe of a lecture, and she let that go by, because she always lets the cheap shots pass like receipts you forget to ask for, and she said, in her real voice now, her plain city voice, You sound bad. Do you have anything in the house. Any ginger ale. Any soup. And I said ginger ale is for children with glamour and I am neither, and besides the bodega man below has a way of unwrapping every bottle like he's auditioning to be my godfather, which I can't handle. The radiator hissed like something Biblical. There was a moth slugging the frosted globe by the hall fixture, throwing out these seedy little eclipses, and I watched it and told her I was tired in the bones, in the expensive, long-named bones nobody thinks about unless they ache. I told her I was receiving, always receiving, this long rain of advice and pity and astonishment, and the umbrella had a hole, and I was drenched and not improved. She said, Buddy--she calls everybody Buddy when she's done talking fancy--Buddy, there isn't any umbrella. There's you, and there's the rain, and sometimes a porch. If you'd like, we can pretend I'm a porch. I went quiet, because that was the one kind of thing she shouldn't be so good at, and there it was, ridiculous and perfect. I said, You'll creak. She said, I'll creak, but I won't collapse. All right, I said, if you must. Be a porch. Be an awning. Be a paper hat. She laughed, and you could hear how she needed me to let her be ridiculous and perfect both, and I don't know what got into me, but I put my feet down on the cold part of the tile, like you do when you're a kid and you want to prove to someone invisible that you can stand it, and I told her to tell me something unimportant, anything absolutely useless, and she said Mrs. Klemper across the way dyed her cat blue for the parade and it rained, so the cat went gray in stripes, and I had to sit right there and not lose my breath laughing, and we were, for a second, two people who had never been told what to do about anything, and the moth quit its heroics, and the radiator went on hissing, and the house held.

Text Passage: June had her elbows on the counter like she was bracing for the kind of weather they name after saints, and the neon over the pie case made the lemon meringue look as if it were having a spiritual experience all by itself; she was fishing a hair out of her lipstick with her thumbnail and asking me (again) if I'd talked to my mother, and I told her (again) that I'd started to, only the line went funny, which wasn't true but felt merciful, and the kid in the paper hat who was pretending to polish the chrome kept not-so-surreptitiously listening in, which was nothing against him--if you're stuck in a diner at four in the afternoon with the coffee burning down to a kind of righteous bitterness, you earn a shot of other people's sorrow--so I let him; I even let him see me try to decide between the tuna melt and something called a Sunshine Special, which was a plate of eggs trying hard to be more than they were. June said I had that look again, the one where I put my jaw out like I'm going to take on the whole block, and I said I didn't know what she was talking about, though I did, because when I told Mr. Cooper that morning that I was leaving the paper--after all that schmoozing for ad space and three perfectly legible features about seniors who knit hats for preemies--I walked past the wire cart with the advance copies and felt like I was wearing a suit two sizes too good for me, which is a feeling that will give you the jaw, believe me. "You can't just leave things," June said, lighting a cigarette with the slow reverence of someone introducing fire to air, and I said I wasn't just leaving, I was quitting specifically, which is different, and she said I was splitting hairs again, and asked if splitting hairs would keep the rent paid, and I told her I'd sell my trumpets (plural, a lie; I have one trumpet and a dented cornet), and she laughed, beautifully, as if I had meant it to be funny, which I hadn't. The bell on the door did this frayed little tinkle and let in a gust that rearranged the napkins; an old man in a hat that might have been respectable twenty years ago came in and ordered coffee like you'd order a pardon, and I watched him fold himself onto a stool and thought unkindly that nobody tells you how much of life is listening to other people clear their throats. Text Passage: I'm not crazy about Saturdays the way people are supposed to be; they always start out like they're going to be marvelous and then they just sit there on your lap like a cat that won't decide whether it loves you or hates you, and your leg falls asleep from the weight of it all. I had this plan where I was going to take the crosstown bus to the park and read something edifying, only the bus was late and half the seats had that gray damp spot nobody ever wants to be responsible for, and my book was one I only like on Tuesdays, if you want the whole miserable truth. I stopped for coffee at this place on Lexington where the cup handles are made for the fingers of saints. The waiter could've been a very nice guy in another life, but in this one he kept looking at his watch like he was timing my adolescence. They had a chalkboard that said Try Our Famous Roll, and nobody was ordering the roll, and it just killed me that some baker in the back was probably praying all morning for somebody to remember the roll even exists. I walked out with my hands in my coat like I had smuggled out mercy, and the air did that flat thing where it makes your cheeks feel like someone's been criticizing them. I cut through the side street with the bleak ficus plants in the apartment lobbies--honestly, those things are held together with tape and faith--and I thought about calling my sister to ask if she wanted to see the turtles at the library pond. She's got this way (Ivy, that's her name) of fixing her hat like she's taking an oath, very solemn, and then laughing a second later because she can't stand being solemn for more than two beats. The truth is, I didn't call. You build these glorious little ideas in your head and then some elevator door in your life closes and there you are waiting all over again, pretending you like elevator music. He looked right at me as if maybe I knew the secret. I pretended I did and showed him how to make a tunnel with your thumbs. He still got mostly spit but he gave this bow like he'd just finished a concerto, and anyway the important part is you do the thing as if there's an orchestra in your pocket. I kept going and looked in a bookstore window, the kind that puts old paperbacks face-out so their wrinkles show. The owner was reading standing up, which I respect in a profound religious way. My brother once sent a postcard from the coast with a picture of a woman in sunglasses and snow, and he wrote, People here pretend it's warm so hard they almost pull it off. He means well. He always means well. My mother left a note on the kitchen counter this morning under the sugar that said Call your father about the keys, and it had a coffee ring on it like a halo, and I folded it and put it in my pocket because I never know when I might need proof that somebody is expecting me to remember something. She was the kind of person who knows exactly where her elbows are. I wanted to tell her not to rush, that the ice doesn't care either way, but you can't go around telling strangers the things they already know about themselves. So I walked to the far path where the low trees act like nosy neighbors and I breathed in that winter garbage smell that nobody ever admits they like, and I thought, if I ever get good at anything, I hope it's carrying a thin paper bag very gently so it doesn't split, because some mornings that's the whole art of being alive, not letting what you've got tear through the bottom before you get it safely home.

Text Passage: The thing that drives me out of my skull lately--besides the mildew that keeps blooming like a cheap renaissance on the bathroom grout--is this boy Klein and his nauseating little genius. I mean it very calmly. Last night at Rubin's I sat through two and a half egg creams and an autopsy of his new novel, which, if there's a God, will never crawl out of its incubator. The kid carries his manuscript around like it's radioactive and he's doing the world a favor by not dropping it, which, incidentally, he never does--he just lays it on the table, dead center, so it can listen to him describe itself. He's got a theory for everything. He's got a theory about forgiveness that starts with penguins and ends with a jazz drummer in a Damascus cellar, and I swear, if I had half his nerve I'd be a saint or an arsonist. He leans in and tells me how he's finally "resolved violence," as if violence had been calling his line all afternoon and he'd just picked up. I told him, as politely as I could manage with my throat closing, that a slap in chapter nine isn't wisdom, it's a slap. He looked wounded--Christ, a glass of milk looks less offended than Klein did--then grinned, because he'd already planned the wounded look, he had it storyboarded. I came home very late and very saintly and found my sister asleep on the sofa with the hissing radio still preaching weather and the cat kneading her ribs like he knew where the doubts were stored. Ma had left a saucer of almonds out, and for a while I ate them one by one like penance and watched the radiator make its little ghost-breaths against the curtain. The city outside was doing its whole interrupted prayer routine--sirens practicing to be trumpets, buses confessing in low gear--and I did that idiotic thing I do, where I try to be both kind and honest at the same time, to people who want neither in the moment they're performing. In the morning, Ma asked if I liked Klein "apart from his act," which is like asking if I like a tiger except for the parts that have teeth. I told her yes, because I'm a coward and also because it's true; sometimes he's funny about his socks not matching, and you can see the exact second the armor gets heavy. I don't know what I'm getting at. There's a little plastic astronaut on my desk, a novelty thing I bought for sixty cents that floats in a transparent dome when you shake it, and I keep shaking it like an absolute lunatic, as if it's going to teach me how to be weightless for five honest minutes. My sister woke up and asked me why I look so tired even when I'm not, and I told her, perfectly cheerfully, "Because I keep trying to forgive people before they've done anything wrong," which sounded slick and therapeutic and not at all like me. She said okay and put the kettle on and scratched the cat exactly between the eyes, with concentration, and I remembered--in a very unliterary stampede--that I love them both in a way that rescues me against my own rotten cleverness, if I let it.

Public opinion on us, in the city where we tried and failed to pass unremarked, was consistently inconsistent; we were either--hands down--the sort of precocious nuisances that give precocity a sulfuric reputation, or we were delicately odd in a way that seemed to license baffled adults to touch our hair. If I'm long-winded, blame the acoustics: the loudspeakers keep promising connection like it's a sacrament, and a man at the next table is catechizing his son's report card with such moral zeal that even the blueberry muffin looks implicated. Text Passage: I was supposed to take Lena to the five-and-dime for a pack of picture hooks, which is the kind of errand my mother invents when the apartment feels crowded with everybody's breath and opinions, and I wasn't too thrilled about it, but Lena had on her red hat with the pom-pom that flops over like it's exhausted from thinking so hard, and you can't leave a person like that to navigate a bell-ringing store by herself, so we went, walking along the salted curb where the ice is chalky and scuffed thin over cigarette butts and bottle caps, and she kept her mittened hand on my sleeve like she was afraid of blowing away, which is something she actually says sometimes, that she might blow away at any minute, and you don't argue with a person who's prepared like that. The cashier is this girl with a heart-shaped birthmark near her jawline, the kind you pretend you didn't see because people get weird when you spot the singular thing about them, but she smiled like she thought we were on some glamorous mission, and Lena kept picking up ridiculous items--stick-on gold stars, a plastic whistle that would mortify God--and telling me how miracles work, one small shiny thing after another until you've got a whole constellation if you don't blink, and I told her she had it wrong, that miracles were the quiet kind that no one claps for, like when you make it across a street and no one dies, and she nodded anyway because Lena is polite even when she's sure you're misinformed. I was thinking about my father in the dentist chair, the way his shoes looked embarrassed on the plastic mat, and how he said he couldn't stand the sound of the polishing thing because it reminded him of radios in bomb shelters (he doesn't tell us where he was, exactly, and I don't press him because there's a smell people give off when they're at the edge and the kindest thing you can do is not fan it), and I almost told the cashier that, can you imagine, unloading that whole messy armful onto the counter with the picture hooks and the whistle, but I kept it to myself and handed her a five, which was too much, but it made me feel like the kind of person who tips fate a little to keep it from sulking. Outside, Lena stopped to watch the bakery guy dust powdered sugar onto these ridiculous little pastries you could inhale in two bites if you were in a hurry to ruin your dinner, and she said we should get one for Mom, but not the jam kind because jam bleeds and it looks like something got hurt, so we got the lemon one that makes your mouth pucker in a way that feels medicinal, and on the way home she told me about a girl in her class who collects the round foil seals from milk jugs and keeps them in a tin that used to hold mints, and how she's saving them for a day when somebody needs proof that miracles are small and round and crinkly, and I said, fine, bring them to my funeral, and Lena rolled her eyes and said I talk like an old man who left his sweater on the bus, and it occurred to me that she was absolutely correct, and that my elbows would always be doing something disreputable no matter how many picture hooks we bought. When we got home, Mom had moved the sofa two inches and claimed the whole room breathed better, which you can't argue with if you happen to love a person, and we ate the lemon thing over the sink, the powdered sugar going everywhere, like weather, and Lena looked up at me with her ridiculous hat and said, very seriously, that she hadn't blown away once, not even a little, and I told her that was the finest miracle I'd ever seen and that we should keep it to ourselves a while longer, the way you cup a match from the wind and pretend your hands are a house.

Text Passage: It was a tired three-forty in the afternoon and the light coming through Lucille's east window had a washed, unhurrying look, as if it had run out of places to be and didn't mind falling on the chipped saucer and the slanted stack of postcards and the one, ridiculous artificial daisy, the kind you pick up at a drugstore because you think you're going to be the kind of person who remembers to dust it. She had the little enamel table pulled up close to the sill, because the radiator was moody and the sill gave off a reasonable impression of warmth, and she was taking exactly forever to finish painting the nails on her right hand. She had decided, a minute ago, not to fret about whether Henry would call before dark--she said it out loud, in a small, officious voice, "Enough of that, Lu," as if anyone with any sense would obey her--and then immediately set the tiny brush down and leaned her head over to look at the street where a man in a brown overcoat was folding himself into a cab like the whole business of traffic and commerce personally bored him. Aunt Maude's hat--elegant felt, a narrow ribbon like something you'd find attached to candy in a better store--sat on the chair back, though Aunt Maude herself was sweeping imaginary crumbs into her hand with the kind of brisk, efficient gestures that make new crumbs appear just from watching. "You can tie yourself into knots if you want," Aunt Maude said, not unkindly, which was the worst, "but hand-wringing never put a nickel in anyone's pocket." "I'm not wringing," Lucille said, tapping her wet thumb against the air like she was testing the mood of a small, invisible pane of glass. "I'm only arranging my nerves." The kettle on the stove had stopped its muttering five minutes ago, which did not prevent Aunt Maude from lifting the lid and setting it back down with proprietary clicks, as if the lid might misbehave while a person's back was turned. The ashtray on the table had achieved that exuberant fullness that suggests history, and Lucille, with her dry hand, slid it an inch away from the lacquer bottle, then another inch, until it sat exactly where it would not telegraph stale smoke to the wet polish. She could feel the phone not ringing in a very specific way, like a yawning toothache of silence, and to prove she wasn't held hostage by it she rose, crossed to the little bookshelf, and corrected the tilt of a paperback she had disliked on principle--so pleased with itself, honestly--even if she'd read the whole thing twice. "If he had anything worth saying, he'd say it," Aunt Maude offered, folding a dish towel lengthwise as if it were a treaty requiring ceremony. "People do what they do when they do it." Lucille liked the sentence less than it deserved to be liked. She thought of Henry's cuff buttons, the heavy ones that said a man had inherited someone's good opinion, and how he'd left one of them--on purpose or not--under the sugar bowl last May, when the windows were open to arguments and music and one specific pigeon with an offended moral stance about everything. "I'm not waiting," Lucille said, and it might have been true for three very cool seconds. Then the hallway door sighed--the building had a talent for sighs--and someone's child moved past in that unpardonable, sock-soft way that makes you want to ring an ankle with bells just for the honesty. Lucille set her thumb under the window's cold sash. She could feel, behind the deliberate drag of each breath, a small, decent part of herself making room, flipping down a cot, straightening the worn cotton sheet of expectation, in case the call decided to come and behave itself.

She was making that open-mouthed declaration face like when she learns a new big word. That ruined and un-ruined me at the same time. The waitress had a pencil through her bun and three tiny hoop earrings stacked up her ear, and she called everyone "hon" with the same resigned bravery you use to pick up a spider with a cup. When I left, it had started that confetti kind of snow, not festive, just indecisive, and I walked with my hands jammed so far into my pockets I was practically inside out. I passed the river where the surface looked like hammered tin and this dog was wearing those booties that make their feet go high, high, like they're in a parade they never agreed to.
