Text Passage: I was supposed to meet my sister at the museum at four, but I got there early because I walked too fast the whole way, like I always do when my head is buzzing with things that don't really deserve all that buzzing, and I kept pretending I didn't care about being early, like being early is some kind of crime you have to hide by looking very professional about it. The guard at the entrance had squeaky shoes and those important eyebrows that make you feel like you need a passport just to breathe, so instead of standing around like I was auditioning to be nervous, I found one of those benches by the big skeleton and sat there, and I tried to look like I had a reason to be there that didn't involve waiting for anybody. There was this boy nearby, small and intent, flipping a penny and catching it, except every third time he'd miss and it would skitter under the radiator and he'd go after it with two fingers, and I liked that about him, that kind of stubborn attention (the penny was dull as a button and not worth all that chasing, but it was his penny, and I respect a person who keeps track of what's theirs). My sister texted me--bus stuck, ten minutes, don't be mad--and I typed back sure, no problem, even though I wasn't mad, not really, just sort of filled up with that drifty feeling you get when your plan shows up late and you realize your plan was never all that reliable to begin with. I was watching people watch the skeleton, and it was incredible how many of them were working hard at looking impressed; you could almost see their faces practicing. A girl with a knitted hat took a photo and then checked it and frowned, like the bones had fallen short on her account. This is going to sound strange, but for a second I wanted to take her phone and say, look up, it's right there, it doesn't need to be rescued into your little glowing square, it's done all its living already. I get like that sometimes (which I know is annoying), where I want to fix the entire world from a bench, with zero qualifications, like I'm the department chair of Common Sense. I checked my reflection in the glass of a display case--it makes your nose look larger and your eyes flatter--and it reminded me of when I was younger and I used to stand in front of this same case with my dad, who always said the same line about how old everything was, older than our arguments, older than our dinners, older than any of the excuses we kept in our pockets. He thought he was being profound, and he was, sort of; I didn't tell him that then, because he would've run with it and I couldn't stand to watch him sprint with truths that were already out of breath. The boy with the penny finally gave up, and he didn't make a big scene about it either; he just stood, brushed his knees, and walked off like the radiator could have it, which is maybe the most admirable thing I saw all day. My sister texted again--five more--and I told her I'd wait as long as it took, which was completely true and made me feel almost heroic, sitting there with my coat on my lap like a folded animal, thinking how most of the decent moments in a person's life are just variations on waiting without pretending you aren't.

I watched the fog on the window bloom with each breath and I wrote his name there with my knuckle and wiped it fast so no one would see, and when we rattled past the field the floodlights were still on, making these serious shadows of the bleachers, like rows and rows of empty teeth, and for a second I got this feeling like if I stepped down off the bus and walked straight into that cold lit-up space I could yell one sharp ordinary word--anything, even something dumb like here--and it would carry, and it would bounce off the metal and come back without breaking, and nobody would tell me to hush or hurry, and nobody would take it away.

Text Passage: I told Miriam, quite calmly, that I wasn't going to turn it into a whole production, and then I did exactly that. It's very hard not to, when you've spent the better part of a winter collecting somebody else's socks from under the radiator and persuading him, like a very patient flight attendant, that his life is not over because his fountain pen exploded during Mercury retrograde. He moved in with me because his sublet "didn't have the right windows" (his phrase, not mine), and I fed him little anchovy toasts and showed him the decent record shops and even let him use my stationery, which is thick enough that you can write furiously and not leave an archaeological imprint four pages down. And then, on Tuesday morning at some ungodly hour, he took off, not like a thief in the night really, because thieves have a kind of professionalism to them, but like a child who suddenly remembers an orthodontist appointment--leaving behind, among other curiosities, one knitted glove and a very damp paperback stuffed with ticket stubs that weren't even mine. He took my scarf though. The charcoal wool one with the narrow herringbone that never quite photographs but feels miraculous on your neck, a small quiet miracle, like folded napkins that come out square the first time. You think I'm petty for mentioning the scarf, but I loved that thing with a somewhat unreasonable love. I am trying to be the sort of person who doesn't love objects unreasonably. It's possible I'm not there yet. I was explaining all this while Miriam stirred her coffee with a little silver spoon that chimed against the cup as if it had rehearsed, and she said, "You're being very composed," which, to be fair, I was practicing. Composure is ninety percent choreography, the other ten percent is remembering not to hurl your napkin in the general direction of the ceiling. The place was loud in the way that makes you think of those diagrams of bees--every table its own tidy hive--and there was a rubber plant in the corner trying very hard to seem sophisticated, and my phone kept doing that soft, pleading buzz like a moth trapped in muslin. He had texted me a photograph of a sunlit staircase in another borough, no caption. I sent back a heart for the sun and a thumbs-up for the staircase, which even I understood was heavy-handed. There is no elegant way to mourn a scarf to someone who's decided they are on a staircase now. Outside, a delivery guy in a plastic poncho did a heroic thing with a dolly and three teetering boxes of lettuce, and a very small boy in a knit hat watched him with that deep animal attention children get when somebody is better at something than anyone else alive. It was snowing but only in a decorative sense, flakes that wouldn't commit. Miriam reached over and, without looking at me, lined up the edge of my saucer with the stripe in the table. It felt like forgiveness, or anyway like a decision not to prosecute. "You're not a doormat," she said. It was kind of her to say so. If you'd been there, you might've seen it too--how the whole room tipped very slightly, as if to allow me to walk out with some shred of ceremony, even if I didn't, even if all I did was fold my hands in my lap and imagine, for an impractical second, the feeling of that scarf, warm and ordinary as a good sentence settling at the back of your throat.

Text Passage: I told my sister it was the worst kind of dream, the slippery-sick kind, and she said, "Don't be dramatic, for God's sake," and then lit a match with her thumbnail in that show-offy way she has, the flame wobbling like it had nerves; she didn't even look at me while she did it, she just flicked ash into the mug where she keeps her hairpins and said, "Proceed," like I was one of her doomed freshmen with their Band-Aid essays and their egos still in the shrink-wrap. The dream, I said, was about the school library, only it wasn't the school library, it was the school library after they'd sunk it under a greenhouse, and there was this vegetation-ish smell everywhere, that too-ripe, breathing-plant smell that makes you feel guilty about how low your pulse is; and the stacks were crammed with glass jars, all the spines floating like pickled fish, and some perspiring custodian kept asking me, with saintly patience, to fetch a blue teapot that had slipped under the lowest shelf, and I had to lie flat and reach into the slick dark, and every time I almost touched it, somebody up above laughed like a spoon hitting tile, and the teapot scooted further in, as if it were actually trying to be good and unfindable. "Freud would faint," my sister said. "Jung would crochet." She has this way of being all-purpose rude that's almost spiritually comforting. Only, listen, I said--I kept wanting to tell whoever was laughing to come down and get their own ridiculous teapot, but my voice wouldn't work; I had all this carefully phrased, sincere-sounding appeal to reason queued up, the whole thing, I swear, like some debate-team monstrosity, and then when I opened my mouth, out came this ghastly polite squeak, like I was the smallest rodent that ever owned a conscience. "That's your regular voice," she said, and grinned sideways, which is darkly charitable of her. I was in her kitchen, if you can call a square of linoleum and a rebellious radiator a kitchen, and the cold made the windows a bad mirror; you could see her face only in the parts where her breath hadn't fogged it over, which, if you're sentimental and very stupid, you can interpret however you please. She was in a sweater so old it had family legends attached, and she had ink on the side of her hand like she'd been thinking with the wrong instrument again. "What is it," she said finally, in this patient, sobered voice she uses when she remembers I have a soul she helped purchase at a yard sale. Inside smelt of damp sugar, paraffin and wet wool. The clerk, a pale boy with pinched lips, took our coupons with a practised indifference, stamped our books with a stamp that had lost its spring, and weighed the margarine as if he were handling contraband. A poster behind his shoulder promised Housebuilding for All and showed a family peeping at a horizon of painted brick; below it, the plaster had fallen in grey petals and revealed a rusted pipe. No one believed the figures but everyone repeated them, in the same way that we repeat the time of day; it is safer to have an answer to hand. The paper I folded under my arm at the counter said that the harvest was the best since records began, and though the grocer's scales slid and stammered when he measured out the flour, the headline, when seen from a distance, still smiled. A constable came in and bought two cigarettes separately wrapped, because that is the rule now, and stared at his own boots as if shocked by how much leather shows when you can no longer afford polish. On the way home I passed the Labour Exchange, whose steps had been worn into two shallow troughs by the feet that climb and descend them; above its door a notice announced a Voluntary Contribution Drive, the only voluntary thing about it being the name. A man with a boil on his neck read it aloud, slowly, like a prayer, and the men to either side nodded without moving their eyes. What makes an untruth most useful is not its size but its tidiness; you can put it in your pocket and forget it is there. Yet even on such mornings small decent acts persist like weeds in cracked concrete. A woman, hands red with suds, stepped out to wedge a bit of cardboard in the mouth of a broken drain so that the children's ankles would not disappear into it; the cat in the doorway blinked with the solemnity of a judge and resigned itself to hunger; a lorry driver lent his thermos to the postman because the canteen tea tasted of coins. It is wrong to say that people enjoy being lied to; they are merely tired, and tiredness, like damp, creeps into the joints of the mind until the effort of straightening up feels like a luxury. I took my loaf and climbed the stairs, counting the landings as one counts the rungs of a ladder lowered into a well. Mrs Evans from Number Five asked, in the tone of one who expects to be deceived but does not care, whether the clocks were going forward or back this week; I gave her the version I had most recently heard. In the scullery the kettle made its small trustworthy racket, and when the steam broke against my face I felt the relief that comes from touching a thing that has not learned to lie.

By the third week the brass plaques had been replaced with new ones: Be Constructive. The next week the slots were narrowed so that envelopes had to be folded once, then twice; in the week after that a gentleman with spectacles explained in the newspaper that folding was a test of sincerity and that only the most heartfelt concerns could be made compact. The door is thick and reluctant; you push it with your shoulder and it sighs as though you were intruding on a secret. Inside there is the usual linoleum, more grey than green, cut and scabbed by heels, and a smell of damp wool and disinfectant which, like cold tea, suggests cleanliness without ever quite achieving it. The chairs are bolted to the floor; the clock is mounted high and briskly five minutes fast; the pencils, such as they are, are tied to the desks with bits of string as though all poverty were a species of larceny. You sit with the others and are numbered in an order nobody explains. Beside me last week a builder's mate with the hands of a navvy--skin split into little white rifts by cement--kept smoothing a creased cap on his knee. When his turn came he was sent away because he had written his middle initial on the wrong line and the girl behind the grille, who looked as if she went home nightly to a room that smelt of face-powder and mutton chops, said, not unkindly but with the finality of a till slamming, that the machine could not swallow muddled answers. After him came a young woman with a baby who hiccupped delicately, like a clock running down; her form was immaculate but her address was not the one on their list. She would have to bring a letter. A system which expects the ruined to be precise is like a hospital that refuses the bleeding until they have scrubbed. Yet nobody here, least of all the clerks, is wicked. They are victims of a superstition subtler and crueller than greed, a faith in Procedure. Efficiency, so called, is the religion of those who have never lifted more than a pen; it abhors the awkward fact and worships the tidy falsehood, and it breeds a style of mind that can balance a column of figures to the farthing but cannot imagine a man without his breakfast. If we wished to help, the method is not abstruse. You would have chairs unbolted and in the right number; you would have the clock honest; you would have one person whose sole business was to explain patiently what is wanted, and you would send nobody away empty-handed if it could be avoided, because hope deferred is as harmful as hunger. You might even give the clients a cup of tea while they wait; though the accountants would cry out, it would save money in the end, for a man who is treated as if he were human is less likely to return snarling at the door. The chairs are bolted to the floor; the clock is mounted high and briskly five minutes fast; the pencils, such as they are, are tied to the desks with bits of string as though all poverty were a species of larceny. You sit with the others and are numbered in an order nobody explains. The corridor inside was painted a pasty green that always suggests someone's idea of economy: coats flaking, pipes sweating, and the noticeboard stuffed with circulars that said Duty and Efficiency and Your Part in the Recovery, the capital letters like iron railings driven into soft ground. The girl behind the glass, with bitten nails and a martyr's patience, passed out small victories--forms accepted, signatures recognised, ration books renewed--and small defeats--applications incomplete, numbers missing, come back next week--without changing the position of her shoulders. In the canteen they were selling something called National Blend which looked like tea and tasted like a rumour; one elderly man, who had the powdered look of someone surviving on boiled opinions, put a dash of milk into his enamel cup and stared at it as if it might declare itself. An advertisement above the urn showed a cheerful family lifting shining forks above a roast of impossible proportions, and beside it another advised that thrift was the new patriotism; the two together made a sort of see-saw on which everyone's stomach rode. Text Passage: At noon the queue had already folded back upon itself twice around the cracked tram-shelter, and the wind that wandered down the avenue of blackened plane-trees carried the smell of wet wool and boiled cabbage like a caution. The loudspeaker on the pole above us droned figures in a pedantic sing-song--more shoes, more coal, more happiness--each numeral round as a plum and as unlikely. People listened without listening. They looked at their boots or the pavement-litter of ticket-stubs and cigarette-ends, measuring out the time by the shuffle forward of a heel or a cough from someone they could not see. A child with a red scarf sucked at a length of string and beat it, solemnly and without purpose, against the railings. I stood there with the rest, my ration book open and damp in the creases, and tried not to think of the taste of tea when there would be none, only the bitter dust that the canteen girl poured and called tea because it came from a brown tin. A poster, pasted crooked on the wall of the bakery, showed a smiling woman with arms like white sausages raising a loaf as if it were an altar-piece. Beneath her a slogan advised us to tighten our belts in the name of prosperity. The paste had bubbled and split across her mouth so that her smile was jagged and full of air. Presently the loudspeaker changed its tone. The announcer spoke about vigilance and gratitude, the two virtues that never cost the treasury a penny. He congratulated the nation for its endurance and thanked us for our patience, which is to say he congratulated himself; for the patience of the governed is the revenue of the governors. Behind me two men argued in whispers over whether the figures were true. One said yes because he wanted to be left in peace. The other said no because it was the only part of his life over which he had any authority. It is a small pleasure to call something a lie and know, to the marrow, that you are correct. Yet even that pleasure is a borrowed one, and when you have spent it there remains the business of walking home with a paper parcel that is lighter than it looks. The queue twitched forward and we moved with the helpless, comic dignity of animals going through a gate. An old woman ahead of me turned and displayed the gap of her mouth like a wound. She said that when she was a girl bread was bread and a promise was something different from a command. I said nothing. There is no answer to that kind of statement except a shrug, and even a shrug can be taken down and used against you. It began to drizzle. The child with the scarf started to cry, not loudly, but as if he had found a note that he could hold forever. When at last I reached the counter the clerk stamped my card without looking up. His hands were raw and cracked, and I felt a foolish sympathy for him, as if we were conspirators in a crime too shabby to name. He handed me a loaf the size of a brick and as soft. As I stepped away the loudspeaker announced that the harvest would be greater still next year. The queue did not laugh. It simply straightened a little, like a man who has learned, over time, to carry a stone in his pocket without limping.

A young mother with a pram studied one that promised training for "new horizons" while her child, with a face both blank and ancient, scraped a button along the pram's metal rim. At the far end there was a desk raised slightly on a platform, and behind it sat a clerk who wore his authority like an extra garment, buttoned up high around the throat. He had a rubber stamp that made a sound which was not loud but final, and he made it often. The people moved forward in small, damp increments. They fumbled in pockets for proofs of existence: a rent book, a gas bill, a letter with a crest. The clerk did not look much at faces. He looked at papers. It is remarkable how a life can be made to fit into boxes on a form if you reduce the print to a small enough size. A man in front of me had the red, wattled look of someone who has put in his years at the foundry and now keeps his hands in his pockets because they are no longer of much use. He said "sir" twice in the space of a sentence, a feint of politeness that was half defiance and half apology. When my turn came I offered up my own little biography: address, date of birth, an account of what I had done to better myself since last being here. I said I had answered advertisements. I said I had made inquiries. The clerk nodded in a way that suggested either agreement or indifference, and I realised it did not matter which. Behind the counter a notice warned that false statements would be prosecuted; beside it another asked for understanding during staff shortages. Both messages had the same brisk handwriting of officialdom, which is to say they were entirely without handwriting at all. The stamp fell again. The room breathed and then held its breath. A man coughed and tried to swallow the cough as if it were contraband. Outside, through the frosted pane, snow fell in the thin way it falls in cities, too tired to stick. You could say that none of this was cruel, not in the way punching is cruel. But there is a slow cruelty in processes that ask you to vanish a little each time you comply. No one wants very much. A kettle that boils without tasting of scale. A chair you can sit in without being noticed. A night in which you are free to be exactly the kind of nobody you are. It would not cost the world much to provide these things. Yet the world, like the clerk, will only give what is asked for in the right words, written in the right boxes, and stamped. When I left, the mother was still at the poster, and the child had fallen asleep with the button in his fist. The snow was already turning to water along the gutter. I felt colder in the daylight than I had inside. It seemed to me that if we are to be saved it will not be by slogans or plans but by the stubborn decency of people who hold a door a second longer than they need to, who share a cigarette, who look you in the face when there is nothing to be gained by it.

Text Passage: When I walk abroad in the morning, and the sun, struggling through the remnant clouds of a nightly tempest, casts its sober lustre alike upon the gilded cornice and the thatch, upon the pavements where the great press idly and the rough lanes where labour hastens, I cannot forbear thinking that truth, like that impartial light, is meant to visit every habitation, though custom would draw curtains before half the human race; for what is this vaunted civilisation, that teaches women to flutter like gaudy insects in a short-lived day, and then to expire in the first keen blast of misfortune, but an elaborate machinery for weakening the very faculties which Providence has given for the perfection of our nature? We talk of delicacy till we blush at sincerity; we teach submission whilst we kindle vanity; we would have the sex persuasive without being wise, tender without being just, and domestic without being citizens--yet how shall the hearth be guarded by those who are not trained to guard themselves? I have seen a girl decked like a nosegay, trembling to recite a sentiment she did not comprehend to an auditor who smiled at her timidity and praised her taste; I have seen, too, a widow, plain as necessity and resolute as duty, who, having measured life by its obligations rather than its ribbons, governed a small household with so much prudence, industry, and unaffected kindness, that every day witnessed the growth of order and content, as a hardy plant, neglected by the florist, takes root in the crevice of a rock and spreads verdure where art had despaired. Which of these, I ask, is fashioned by a rational education? The former is strung like a lute to the caprice of an idle hand; the latter draws harmony from the firm touch of principle. It will be said that gentleness is the character of woman--granted, if by gentleness we mean that softness of heart which tempers justice, not that feeble pliancy which yields to every imposition; but gentleness is the blossom of strength, not the sickly efflorescence of dependence. Make women free in mind, and you will find them faithful in affection; teach them to respect themselves, and you need not fear that they will worship trifles. A being who has never been accustomed to consider consequences, who has been hurried from fancy to fancy as from room to room in a gaudy mansion, cannot be expected to act with steadiness when the house itself shakes; and society, which had amused her with toys, will then reproach her childish tears. Oh, let us have done with this mock homage paid to their weakness; it corrupts the strong, and it kills the weak. Give them a portion of the rough fare of truth, of the plain bread of knowledge, and they will not solicit the sugared poison that now inflames the imagination whilst it withers the heart. I address not men as tyrants, but as brothers; do you wish for companions rather than playthings, mothers rather than nurses, friends rather than flatterers? Then, in the name of that reason which ennobles us all, suffer not female virtue to be confounded with a trick of manners, nor female piety with a hectic enthusiasm; let the same standard of duty be erected for both, and the same paths of honour be trodden. The branch smitten by lightning puts forth, in a happier season, sounder shoots than those which were fostered in perpetual shade; thus will character, braced by difficulty and invigorated by exercise, bring forth the sober fruits of liberty--temperance, fortitude, and benevolence--which alone can render private life a school of public good.

Text Passage: Among the many illusions with which society beguiles the unwary, none appears to me more fatal than that soft tyranny which, under the specious names of delicacy and refinement, would confine women to an ignoble sphere, persuading them that to charm is a higher duty than to think, and to obey more graceful than to act. I have observed, with a mixture of sorrow and indignation, that the gossamer threads of praise which are cast about the young--those light applauses that attend a nimble step, a well-turned compliment, or a studied blush--soon become cords, and at length iron chains; for flattery paralyses the very faculties it pretends to celebrate, and, whilst it pretends to protect, seduces the mind from the severer exercise of her own powers. What wonder, then, if we find that an understanding never tasked for truth grows peevish under contradiction, and a heart trained to catch every breeze of approbation becomes the sport of caprice? Men, it is said, are the legislators of opinion; but, alas! they are often themselves its subjects, bowing to the despotism of custom with as blind a submission as the very beings whom they accuse of frivolity; and so the circle of folly is perpetuated, each sex reflecting the weakness of the other, till reason, like a slighted tutor, is dismissed from the household. Would it not be more consonant with the dignity of our nature, and more favourable to domestic felicity as well as public virtue, to cultivate in women that sober independence which springs from a well-instructed judgment? Teach a girl to measure praise by principle, not principle by praise; habituate her, from the dawn of life, to examine before she assents, to resist before she relishes, to prefer the solid peace of self-approbation to the glitter of transient notice; and you will not find her, when the flower of novelty is shed, a restless trifler, but a companion, a friend, a citizen. Let not mothers be told that such discipline will sour the temper, or impair those softer graces which give the domestic affections their charm; for true tenderness is the daughter of strength, and only the firm mind can afford to be gentle. What is called sensibility, when unregulated, evaporates in tears and prettiness, leaving duty undone and sorrow unrelieved; whereas the affections that have been chastened by thought grow active and enduring, and their very fervour is a pledge of perseverance. Text Passage: I have frequently been told, with an air of triumph, that the glory of our age consists not in the rude energies of uncultivated minds, but in that refined sensibility which, like a polished mirror, catches each trembling beam of pleasure and pain; yet I cannot help observing that a mirror, though it reflect light, generates none, and that the heart which is made the slave of every transient impression seldom learns to obey the steady dictates of reason or the sober voice of duty. What do we gain by training a young woman to be the plaything of an indolent hour, bidding her smile when caprice beckons and weep when vanity is not flattered, if, when the storm of fortune rises, she can neither guide her own vessel nor assist a struggling companion? Is it not mockery to praise female softness while corrupting the very source of fortitude, to load the altar of delicacy with flowers whilst the sacrificial victim is reason, bound and veiled? We talk loudly of national vigor, of the independence that should ennoble a free people, and yet we stifle the first breath of independence in half the species, decking out their weakness with names that would disgrace the most childish bauble; for what is this boasted modesty, if it be but prudery that fears the truth; what this winning obedience, if it be but a habit of servile assent learned in the nursery and practised in the drawing-room? I would rather see a daughter taught to question than to curtsy, to revere principle rather than persons, and to discipline her affections till they become the auxiliaries, not the tyrants, of her understanding; for affection, unguided, is but a torrent in spate, beautiful in its spray and sound, yet destructive of the meadows it was meant to fertilize. It will be said that the gentler virtues perish beneath the stern eye of truth; but I have found the contrary, that tenderness, when it grows on the stock of judgment, becomes charity, and that constancy, when it is the habit of a cultivated mind, secures that peace which petulant sensibility perpetually forfeits. Let mothers, then, cease to dress their children for the masquerade of life, teaching them attitudes when they should form principles; let the needle no longer be the sceptre of their empire, nor the dance the passport to their hopes; give them books that exercise the mind rather than trinkets that enchain the fancy; suffer them to climb the hill of difficulty and to feel the wholesome cold of the morning, that their blood may be pure and their spirits enterprising; and do not whisper in their ear that dependence is protection, when it is but a decent name for bondage, nor that fortune will provide, when diligence and integrity are the only sure inheritances. If, in pleading thus, I am thought severe, it is because I would save my sex from the severer judgment of events; for life, that unflattering preceptor, soon tears away the gauze of factitious charms, and then the woman who has lived for opinions, starved of convictions, finds that the applause of an hour is a poor substitute for the calm of a well-governed soul. Let us then, with a courage buoyed by humility, resolve to be what we are capable of becoming, creatures of reason, candidates for virtue, companions in the labor of improvement; so shall domestic affection be no longer a childish play, but a solemn fellowship; and public happiness, that great edifice which totters while its foundation is sand, may rest at last upon a broader basis, cemented by justice and enlightened by truth.

Text Passage: I have often observed, with a mixture of indignation and melancholy, that the very minds which most boast of delicacy are those that have never been trained to endure the wholesome severities of truth; they shrink from argument as from inclement air, and, mistaking the thrill of a transient sensation for the steady fire of conviction, they surrender their judgment to the nearest flatterer who will consent to dignify their caprice with the name of sentiment. Our daughters are disciplined to become pleasing rather than principled; our sons are exhorted to be daring rather than just; and thus the domestic hearth is converted into a little court, where pertness passes for wit, obsequiousness for good-breeding, and where sincerity, daring to appear without a ribbon, is rudely dismissed as unfit for company. Shall we wonder that public liberty totters when private virtue is thus undermined? A nation cannot be free whilst its households are scenes of petty despotism, where the weaker learn artifice for defense and the stronger learn arrogance for rule; for whoever is tyrant at home will be a poor guardian of rights abroad. Let us begin, then, with the alphabet of morals, and teach the young to reverence their own faculties; to prefer a just reproof to a sweet falsehood; to bear disappointment without peevishness, and success without intoxication; to feel that the applause of fools is a wind that chills, whilst the approbation of conscience warms like a durable sun. Accustom them to plainness in dress and frankness in speech, that the apparel of virtue may not be mistaken for her essence; bid them exert their limbs in the brisk service of health, for a vigorous frame lends stability to thought, and the same habits which brace the body fortify the understanding. Lead them into the fields, not merely to cull gaudy flowers which fade before noon, but to trace the grave constancy of the seasons, to bless the impartial bounty of the dawn, and to learn that nature's stern lessons are but the scaffolding of joy. Let conversation be a gymnasium rather than a parade; let books be companions, not sedatives; and let religion, brightened by inquiry, become a living principle instead of a tremulous superstition sought only in danger and forgotten in ease. With such foundations, affection will cease to be that feverish barter of vanities which disgraces the holy name of love; marriages will be formed on the union of minds, and friendship, that severest friendship which dares admonition, will prove the only soil in which passion ripens into felicity. I am not ignorant that the worldly-wise will call this earnestness romantic, and commend their safer craft of training compliant dolls and ambitious triflers; but I have seen the harvest of that policy--discontent masked by laughter, indulgence breeding more hunger than it appeases, and an age powdered into finery while the heart starves. Present to a child one example of fortitude, one instance where convenience was not suffered to dethrone conscience, one confession of fault made without excuse, and you will have taught more than by a thousand proverbs dictated with a frown. Courage, then; for if women be educated into rational companions rather than glittering playthings, and men learn the tenderness of strength rather than the softness of servility, we shall yet rescue domestic life from its gilded littleness, and civil life from its gaudy bondage; else ribbons will still be preferred to laurels, and the republic of souls be peopled by dwarfs.

Text Passage: It has often occurred to me, while contemplating the variegated scene of human life, that the most dangerous fetters are those which a smiling hand adjusts, and that the tyranny of Opinion--decked out in garlands and trinkets--sits more securely on the neck than the iron despotism against which men sometimes rouse themselves to act; for who shall be provoked to fling away a chain that looks like an ornament, or to suspect poison in the draught that sparkles with a benignant light? I lately observed, in a saloon where every sense was seduced into indolence, a youthful creature, pliant as the ribbon at her breast, taught to smile before she could reason, and to cast down her eyes before she had any thoughts to hide; and I was told, by those who had the training of her, that she was to make a figure in the world, that her destiny was to charm, and, by that soft witchery which knows not its own end, to ride safely through life upon the opinions of others, as a light bark is carried by a summer current. Yet, the same day, I paused at the threshold of a lowly dwelling, poor in every external appendage except neatness and order, and beheld a woman whose weather-stained hands had learned the alphabet of labor, and whose brow, fretted rather by care than vanity, was calm with the security of principles made habitual by exercise; and I asked myself--was not her heart more likely to expand in genuine benevolence than that of the fine idol whose imagination, fed with showy images and little precepts, fluttered without resting upon any truth, like a gaudy insect that dies with the evening? For what, I beseech you, is the foundation of respectability, if not the steady exercise of reason; and how shall reason be exercised, if we never permit it to try its strength, but confine it to the petty circle of graceful compliance, trivial accomplishments, and a scrupulous attention to appearances, which are, at best, but the shadows of virtue? I know it will be said by some, who, by a false delicacy, term pusillanimity refinement, that to awaken the mind is to disturb the peace of domestic life; as if a peace that must be purchased by the abdication of a rational creature's prerogative were not a specious calm, under which all the nobler powers languish into imbecility. Let us be just; if women are to be held responsible for the morals of the world--an office perpetually laid at their door by those who deny them the instruments of fulfilling it--then, surely, we ought rather to brace than to relax their faculties; to make them friends than idols; companions in truth, not playthings of fancy. I would have my sex taught to stand upright, that their benevolence may be active, not coaxing; their tenderness the offspring of principle, not the sickly child of servile fear; and their love, whether given to man or to humanity, the sober enthusiasm of a mind that discerns the good, not the blind attachment of a heart that clings because it cannot walk. Believe me, a character disciplined by thought will carry cheerfulness into the humblest duties, as the sun gladdens the cottage no less than the palace; while that sickly bloom of sensibility, which fashion cherishes as the very rose of life, fades at the first rough visitation--leaving nothing but paleness, vacuity, and caprice, where a fortitude, nourished by truth, might have reared a harvest of lasting joys.

Text Passage: Contemplate, my countrywomen, the daily farce which the world, with grave folly, dignifies by the name of education, and then tell me whether a rational creature can be formed amidst such tinkling ornaments and feverish vanities; for is it not notorious that the girl is taught to move before she is taught to think, to shine before she is capable of discerning the nature of true light? She is led, as with satin cords, through apartments where every mirror multiplies her dependence, and every smile that meets her is but a polished chain; and thus habituated to receive homage without earning respect, she grows familiar with a species of tyranny that makes her, in turn, the most docile of slaves. I have no harsh quarrel with graceful deportment, nor with the decent care that health and cleanliness exact; but when these lighter graces are exalted into sovereign virtues, when the needle is preferred to the book and the fluttering of a fan over the exercise of judgment, what result can be expected, save that we rear delicate triflers who bend to the breeze of opinion, and who, having never been taught to consult the steady oracles of reason, mistake caprice for wisdom? Tell me, mothers, who ought most to venerate truth, you upon whose bosoms an infant first reads the character of this world, are you content to see your daughters embellished into insignificance, their principles ribboned and their minds laced as tightly as their stays? The nation that neglects to furnish its women with the robust furniture of thought must not wonder if its men grow feeble in the very part wherein strength is most required; for domestic society is the nursery of public spirit, and there is no freedom in the state where despotism, however smiling, rules at the fireside. By what strange perversion have we come to applaud sensibility when it dissolves duty, to crown nerves with laurel and send judgment supperless to bed? Virtue, like a hardy plant, loves the wholesome air of difficulties; it is not cherished under glass, nor coaxed by perfumers' breath; and she who has never been suffered to err can scarcely learn to correct herself. I would have every woman accustom her mind to the patient analysis of causes, to disengage truth from the tinsel of authority, to prefer a modest conviction to a loud assent; she will then cease to barter conscience for caresses, and to purchase a shadowy protection by the surrender of her understanding. Let affection be the companion of esteem, not its gaoler; let marriage be a congress of minds, not a treaty for the maintenance of extravagance; and then, when the inevitable storms of life beat against the dwelling, will not the hearth be warmer because a reasonable friend presides there, not a fretful idol craving incense? Reform, I entreat you, begins not in the closet of legislators but at the cradle; and she who reads with her child, who teaches him to reverence what is right because it is right, builds with firmer materials than those who traffic in maxims stitched on cushions. Train the heart by disciplining the head; the former, left to ungoverned emotion, will, like an ill-managed horse, dash both rider and carriage into the mire; but reason, quietly holding the rein, leads steadily along the road where honor pays its tolls and liberty keeps the milestones.

Text Passage: It has long appeared to me a species of domestic treason, as well as public folly, that we should prefer the shadow of virtue to its substance, and suffer the daughters of our country to be trained, like minstrels at a feast, to charm the ear while the understanding lies dormant; for what hope can a nation entertain of durable freedom, when half its members are educated to revere opinion rather than truth, to court protection rather than exercise judgment, and to purchase a precarious influence with the brittle coin of personal allurements? I am not insensible to the delights of gentleness, nor do I deny that grace is an agreeable attendant upon worth; but when gentleness is cultivated to enfeeble, and grace exalted above rectitude, then we manufacture not women, but apparitions--things that glitter and deceive, and vanish at the first rude breath of adversity. The tyranny which men exercise over women in thus shaping their minds to servility is not merely a moral crime, it is also a political blunder; for the domestic circle is the primary school of citizenship, and where the earliest lessons are apology, compliance, and a scrupulous attention to trifles, the grown learner will be but ill prepared to practise fortitude, sincerity, and public spirit. Let us, therefore, cease to confound delicacy with virtue, and to applaud that sensibility which, unharnessed by principle, proves only an instrument of self-love, quick to resent and quicker still to yield, elastic to temptation, and querulous under duty. I desire not to unsex women by inviting them to usurpations that neither suit their situation nor adorn their character; I desire only that, as rational creatures accountable to the same moral Lawgiver, they should be habituated to think, to will, and to act from motives that bear examination; that they should be encouraged to strengthen the sinews of the mind as carefully as the muscles of the body are nursed by capricious indulgence; that they should taste of simple pleasures, acquire plain knowledge, and associate that knowledge with practice, so that they may love truth for its own austere beauty. A mother thus enlightened will not, like a gaoler whose interest is in weakness, keep her child chained by fear and ornamented by folly; she will rather require veracity before politeness, perseverance before elegance, and modesty as the bloom of a sound root, not as a paint spread to delude the eye. Nor will a man, who respects himself as a citizen rather than a despot, desire in his companion the mute complacency that betrays a sluggish conscience; he will seek a friend with whom he may take counsel in prosperity and receive rebuke in error; for, believe me, that marriage is most tender where it is most reasonable, and respect is its surest cement. To such a reform, ridicule and clamour will, doubtless, oppose their ancient artillery; yet when were improvements achieved by those who feared a laugh? If we would have daughters firm without harshness, affectionate without servility, and pious without superstition, we must open to them the clear pathways of principle, and suffer them to tread there with a steady step, even if the embroidery of their slippers be somewhat soiled. Then, and not till then, shall we see domestic peace allied to public virtue, and the private hearth warming the commonwealth with a rational and manly--shall I not say womanly?--flame.

Text Passage: This morning, when the sun, struggling through a mantle of grey vapour, only glimmered upon the river as upon a conscience half-awakened, I walked forth to commune with that plain Nature which never flatters folly, and I felt anew how perverse is the education that seduces women from her frank lessons to the gewgaws of opinion. The reeds bowed with a sober grace, not seeking admiration yet graceful because they obeyed the wind without affectation; and, contemplating their undulation, I could not help contrasting it with that studied pliancy which modern discipline exacts from my sex, who are taught to bend, not to principles, but to every caprice of fashion and every petty despotism of domestic caprice. Must we, I asked, call those virtues which are but dexterous cowardices? For is it courage to purchase a poor security by the sacrifice of sincerity; wisdom to barter the growth of the understanding for the brittle triumph of a transient smile? I have been told, till my ear is weary, that gentleness is the diadem of woman; but I discern in this flattery the stamp of tyranny; for when the name of a jewel is bestowed on a fetter, it is only that the captive may learn to kiss her chain. Believe me, my friend, the only gentleness worth possessing is that which springs from self-command and the habit of justice; and these are not the spoils of indolence, but the harvest of labour. Let the faculties be put to their proper use; let the affections, pruned by Reason not clipped by fear, branch out in their natural directions; let conscience, that faithful sentinel, be trained to distinguish the call of duty from the whispers of vanity; then, and not till then, will the character acquire that composure which can bear the day's heat and the night's solitude. I have observed in the cottages that border this stream a rude but honest economy; the mother spins while the child learns, in the very sight of labour, that happiness is not a banquet spread by unseen hands, but the sober meal prepared by industry and seasoned by hope. How superior is this tuition to the sickly refinements of the drawing-room, where fancy is tasked to invent wants, and sensibility, pampered to a fever, expires at the slightest disappointment! Oh, that parents would dare to respect their daughters as rational creatures, and seek rather to render them estimable than admired; for admiration, hungry and clamorous, devours the very nutriment of excellence, whilst esteem, patient and steadfast, nourishes it. Were women early accustomed to compare the tumult of passion with the serenity of principle; to feel, in the presence of mountains and storms and labouring men, the insignificance of costume and the majesty of truth; they would cease to revere gilded wrongs and would learn to reverence themselves. Can society, thus improved, be less graceful? Will tenderness be banished because sincerity is enthroned? No; for the heart, once relieved from the ignoble necessity of dissembling, expands with a generosity unknown to the slave of opinion; and friendship, entering by the gate of respect, will not flee at the first chill of adversity. Let us then have done with gingerbread idols and the perfumed incense of fools; let us seek, in plain air and honest studies, the sustenance of the soul, until, like the river now brightening into day, our lives, no longer creeping between low banks of custom, widen and shine in freedom.

Text Passage: If it be asked why I grow earnest upon a topic which the most ordinary observation might decide, I would answer that this very plainness is the cause of my indignation; for, walking but yesterday along the damp margin of a little green where children were permitted to frisk only within the measured bounds their governess had traced with her parasol, I saw a timid girl, her eyes lifted with an eager light to the clouds that sailed like islands of liberty above her, rebuked for venturing one step beyond the chalked circle; the offence was trivial, yet the punishment--the long moral harangue on becoming softness, on the peril of stained shoes and a flushed cheek--fell on her like a cold rain that beats back the bud. Are we, who confess ourselves the disciples of reason, to persist in such petty tyrannies, and then wonder that the human mind, so hedged in, brings forth but sickly fruit? We pretend to cherish delicacy when we are only cultivating weakness; we call it prudence to teach submission before principle, and we imagine that a creature trained to start at a shadow will stand firm before a real danger. It is vain to varnish the chain with roses; its weight is not thereby lightened. I have been told--by men who speak of women as if they were waxen figures to be moulded by flattery--that retirement polishes the heart, and a long tutelage of trifles refines the taste; I deny it. Virtue, like the hardy plant which strikes its roots where the winds are roughest, gathers strength from exertion; it is not a hothouse flower, grateful only to a tepid atmosphere and the hand that waters it with tears. Let us cease to mistake caprice for sensibility, pliancy for good nature, coquetry for tenderness; let us rather demand in our daughters, and by consequence secure in our sons, that steady love of truth which can endure contradiction, that active habit of self-command which, practised in the small concerns of the day, becomes at length the guardian of principle in the great. If love must be propped on ignorance, then human felicity is a phantom; if marriage require for its support that one party be a slave and the other a master drunken with a little brief authority, then domestic peace is but a truce signed under the flag of fear. Far otherwise do I conceive the holy league of minds; friendship is its foundation, esteem the cement, and rational liberty the roof beneath which tenderness may dwell secure. I appeal to mothers who tremble when their children cough, yet hazard, by perpetual surveillance, the nobler health of the soul; to legislators who would have the state flourish without admitting half the citizens to the rights of improvement; to men of gallantry who would prove their devotion by preventing the very growth that would render women worthy of it. Suffer them to read, to labour, to err and rise again; permit them some share in the world's business beyond the embroidery frame and the sick-bed; and you shall find, I dare assert, that they return to the hearth, not less gentle, but more firm; not less affectionate, but more just; for they will bring home the consciousness of a being exercised, not wasted; and the smile which springs from a mind at peace with itself hath a serenity that the most artful grimace can never counterfeit. Let us aim, in fine, at forming creatures whose respect we may covet, not dependants whose praise is a tax; and we shall at last discover that the only ornament which time does not tarnish is a character strengthened by truth.

We pretend to cherish delicacy when we are only cultivating weakness; we call it prudence to teach submission before principle, and we imagine that a creature trained to start at a shadow will stand firm before a real danger. It is vain to varnish the chain with roses; its weight is not thereby lightened. I have been told--by men who speak of women as if they were waxen figures to be moulded by flattery--that retirement polishes the heart, and a long tutelage of trifles refines the taste; I deny it. Virtue, like the hardy plant which strikes its roots where the winds are roughest, gathers strength from exertion; it is not a hothouse flower, grateful only to a tepid atmosphere and the hand that waters it with tears. Let us cease to mistake caprice for sensibility, pliancy for good nature, coquetry for tenderness; let us rather demand in our daughters, and by consequence secure in our sons, that steady love of truth which can endure contradiction, that active habit of self-command which, practised in the small concerns of the day, becomes at length the guardian of principle in the great. If love must be propped on ignorance, then human felicity is a phantom; if marriage require for its support that one party be a slave and the other a master drunken with a little brief authority, then domestic peace is but a truce signed under the flag of fear. Far otherwise do I conceive the holy league of minds; friendship is its foundation, esteem the cement, and rational liberty the roof beneath which tenderness may dwell secure. I appeal to mothers who tremble when their children cough, yet hazard, by perpetual surveillance, the nobler health of the soul; to legislators who would have the state flourish without admitting half the citizens to the rights of improvement; to men of gallantry who would prove their devotion by preventing the very growth that would render women worthy of it. Suffer them to read, to labour, to err and rise again; permit them some share in the world's business beyond the embroidery frame and the sick-bed; and you shall find, I dare assert, that they return to the hearth, not less gentle, but more firm; not less affectionate, but more just; for they will bring home the consciousness of a being exercised, not wasted; and the smile which springs from a mind at peace with itself hath a serenity that the most artful grimace can never counterfeit. Let us aim, in fine, at forming creatures whose respect we may covet, not dependants whose praise is a tax; and we shall at last discover that the only ornament which time does not tarnish is a character strengthened by truth.

Text Passage: At that sober hour when the household is yet hushed, and the pale herald of day steals modestly through the uncurtained window, I often turn my thoughts, not to those trifling decorations which the world esteems, but to the discipline by which a rational creature is fitted to act with dignity in every scene of life; and then, surveying the actual state of female education, I am compelled to ask whether we are training women to be steady companions and useful citizens, or but pliant ornaments, fluttering in the sunshine of caprice, and withering at the first breath of adversity. The fashion of the day, which lulls the conscience with its lisping flatteries, would persuade us that a soft voice, a pliant temper, a ready smile, and an air drilled into decorum, are graces sufficient to insure happiness; yet experience, that stern monitor who will not be bribed, daily pronounces a contrary verdict, for the charities of home, like the virtues of public life, are not born of vanities, but of a mind accustomed to weigh reasons, to forgo present indulgence for lasting good, and to esteem truth above the painted semblances that pass for it in the market of reputation. I speak not harshly of the sex when I affirm that they are too often taught to anticipate protection rather than to procure self-respect, for, whilst their hands are exercised in every dainty art that catches the eye, their understandings are left uncultivated, and their hearts rendered the sport of every amiable error which, for want of examination, usurps the name of virtue. What wonder if, reared amidst incense, they become fastidious worshippers at the altar that perfumes them, and turn with disgust from the homely labours by which households flourish and nations are sustained? Yet surely it is no paradox to maintain that a woman will preside most gracefully over the tender charities of life when she has learned to govern herself; that she will best cherish children when she can respect the faculties that are awakening in them; and that she will most truly love her husband when she stands by his side, not as an echo of his prejudices, but as the firm friend of his reason and the vigilant guardian of his moral peace. To this end let her be accustomed betimes to encounter difficulty, to relish the victories of patient study, to trace effects to causes, and to distinguish that solid happiness which springs from an upright course from the feverish raptures of applause; for taste is a fugitive visiter, virtue a constant inmate. I would not banish accomplishments, but subordinate them; I would have the needle ply while the judgment argues, the fingers move while the conscience dictates; I would have the mind instructed to furnish precepts, that the hand may execute purposes worthy of an immortal being. When once such habits are formed, the gilded tyranny of opinion will lose its sceptre; the mother will cease to barter her child's future for a tinsel hour; the daughter will prefer a plain truth to an insidious compliment; and both, emerging from the bondage which confounds weakness with delicacy, will display that native strength which, like the oak braced by rough winds, roots itself the deeper for the storm, and spreads a shade under which private felicity and public virtue may grow together.

Text Passage: This morning, as I paced with rapid step along the river's margin, while the vapours yet hung upon the meadows, and the first stir of labour was audible in the clatter of the distant mill, I could not refrain from musing on that species of refinement which, like a gauze thrown over the faculties, dims instead of exalting them; for I beheld a young mother tripping lightly, her garments contrived with a studied negligence to bespeak delicacy rather than health, pressing to her side a child that importuned with that honest eagerness which wants a guide, not a flatterer. She hushed him with sugared phrases, as though truth were too coarse a morsel for infant lips, and when his little feet would have run towards the open field, she gently checked him, fearing the stain of grass upon his shoes more than the rust of indolence upon his spirit. In the same moment a pale seamstress, whose back was bent by unremitting toil, raised her eyes from the window where she sat imprisoned as in a shrine to Fashion, and their hollow brightness seemed to ask by what right the one sex should be inflated with fictitious consequence whilst the other is taught to steal it, like a furtive light, from admiration purchased at the expense of sense. Let it not be imagined that I would overturn any mild and social decorum which preserves the sweetness of domestic life; I only contend that the flower which is pruned into dwarfish grace will neither shelter the traveller nor feed the hive. If we would have citizens, we must first have creatures capable of standing alone in the honest daylight of reason; and if women are expected to form the minds of men, ought they not first to establish their own upon principles broad as truth and firm as virtue? Yet what do we behold? A childish play of desires, a commerce of smiles and sighs, the understanding kept as a page to caprice, and the conscience lulled with lullabies of reputation; whilst the body, tenderly wrapped, grows languid beneath its finery, and the heart, denied robust exercise, mistakes agitation for sentiment, and vanity for benevolence. I am weary of hearing that our softness is our sceptre, and our ignorance our charm; for what despot ever forged a fetter more secure than that which the captive polishes with complacency? Believe me, affection is most sacred when it is most rational; a friendship with duty at its core will outlast those transient ecstasies which sparkle like meteors only to vanish and leave darkness more profound. Let us, then, teach our daughters to climb hills, to read books not for the tinsel of phrases but for the sinew of thought, to speak truth without grimace and to succour distress without theatre; let us shew them that plainness of dress may consist with opulence of mind, and that the blush of exertion is a fairer rouge than any compounded by art. Then, when a tempest shakes the household, they will not cling in helpless terror to the nearest arm, but, collected and serene, will consult reason as their pilot; and the children, beholding this composure, will learn to reverence what sustains, rather than what merely captivates. For indeed, if freedom is any blessing, it must be that dominion which every creature may secure within--a sovereignty over prejudice, fear, and the seductions of idle praise; and such empire, founded upon knowledge and exercised in habitual virtue, is the only diadem that neither tyrant nor season can wrest away.

Text Passage: I have been often accused, with a sort of compassionate disdain that wounds more than open hostility, of labouring to unsex the delicate drudges of our drawing-rooms; yet, when I inquire whether delicacy that depends on ignorance be not a badge of bondage rather than a charm of virtue, I am met with smiles that would fain pass for argument, and with scraps of maxims, as brittle as the porcelain hearts they decorate. What, I ask, is the use of a life made up of attitudes? To flutter, to fade, to be praised where one ought to be respected, and courted where one longs to be considered--are these the triumphs that ought to content an immortal spirit? The appetite for flattery is but the dyspepsia of a mind starved of solid nourishment; and she who, bereft of principles, clings to opinion as to a reed on a torrent, shall feel it pierce her hand when the flood of mischance runs strong. I would have woman trained, not as a toy, not as the minister to paltry vanities, but as the fellow-labourer in every rational good, the vigilant guardian of her own integrity, the friend and equal of man; for without equality there can be no friendship, and without friendship affection is a fever that exhausts rather than strengthens. Let them grant us the use of our faculties, and we will pledge our lives to supply the evidence of our capacity; for reason is no monopolist, admitting of no charter save that which Nature and God have sealed upon the human countenance. It is true, perhaps, that sensibility, unguided by thought, spreads a glittering veil over folly; but the same sensibility, disciplined by reflection and exercised by duty, will refine benevolence into justice, and expand partial tenderness into an affection for universal good. If I speak warmly, it is because I would snatch from the altar of Pride those garlands of spurious praise that have long been hung about the necks of weakly idolized women, until, strangled by their very honours, they have sunk into a grave where memory blushes to weep. The tyranny of opinion, that invisible scepter shaken from nursery to nuptial-bed, exacts compliance in the very tone of the voice and the fold of the garment; yet it never asks for the courage to choose right when right is solitary. Shall the soul be schooled in smiles rather than in maxims? Shall a mind, meant to weigh consequences and to embrace truth, be taught only to catch the accents of command or the whispers of applause? I have watched a mother, penning decked sentences to placate some heartless censor of her household, while her child's eye, inquisitive and bright, sought nourishment more bracing than sugared restrictions; and I thought, if that little being were nurtured to think, to act, to dare in the cause of right, how much domestic peace would lose its flimsy ornaments to gain the comely vesture of virtue! Economy without meanness, gentleness without servility, fortitude without ferocity--these are the graces I covet for my sex; not the painted bloom that the first wind of fortune scatters, but the inward health of principle, which, like the hardy plants of our own fields, takes root the deeper when the air is sharp and the soil unkind.

Text Passage: It has long appeared to me, whilst I have observed with equal attention the humbler cottages and the gilded parlours through which my course has accidentally led me, that the grand misfortune of my sex is less a natural defect than an artificial misdirection; for instead of being accustomed, from the dawn of life, to weigh motives, to compare duties, and to feel that dignity of conscious rectitude which no outward ornament can bestow, we are taught, with a solicitude that ill deserves the venerable name of care, to prize the minute graces that catch a vagrant eye, to value a trembling softness that precludes exertion, and to believe that the highest exercise of understanding is to read the glance of a superior whom flattery has transformed into a species of oracle. How, I ask, shall a nation be free, if the very nursery is the school of dependence? I am not insensible to the mild delights of domestic affection--indeed, I revere them as the sacred bond of social happiness--but I cannot honor that counterfeit union which rests only on the vigilant management of trifles and the artful concealment of thought; for a harmony that trembles at the touch of reason is more a truce than a friendship. When, in a solitary walk at sunrise, I have watched the laborer advance with measured step to his task, and heard, amidst the quiet stir of awakening fields, some mother's voice modulating the first sounds of speech in her child, I have felt my heart glow with a hope that the moral world might one day be thus industrious, thus serene; yet straightway the scene is clouded by a recollection of those drawing-rooms where young minds are taught to mistake volatility for wit, compliance for grace, and dissimulation for prudence, till the very name of virtue is narrowed into the pale semblance of decorum. Let men boast no longer of the tender empire they maintain by such means; for it is a poor dominion that exacts homage from weakness, and fearful is the price they pay who purchase submission at the expense of truth. The mask they bind on another's face clings closer to their own; feeble counsellors make feeble companions; and the frivolity they applaud at home reacts upon the state, till laws themselves grow as capricious as the manners which support them. Text Passage: They crossed the flats at first light, man and burro, and the day came on raw and colorless as bone and the wind walked the salt scabs and the ragwort and stirred a tin can that clacked and spun and lay mute again, and there were no other travelers upon that waste save a skein of black birds riding the sheared air to no certain end. He kept his hat brim low and his eyes on the far rise where the land swelled as if to conjure a shore that had long ago drowned, and in the low hollows the last of winter's water lay rank and slick as oil with a film that held the sky without reflecting it and the prints of coyotes stitched the margins like a crude embroidery. They passed a windmill with two blades torn away and the shaft locked so that it faced forever a quarter of the compass it had not chosen, and below it a tank of corrugated steel whose ring was crusted with alkali that flaked when the burro nosed it and took nothing for its trouble but the taste of iron. In the man's pocket a square of oilcloth held a scatter of cartridges and a shard of mirror and a nail bent into the shape of a fish, keepsakes of a former scripture, and sometimes when the land turned empty in a new way he would thumb them and know they held no more grace than a handful of dirt and maybe less and he would let them go again. The road was not a road but the ghost of one, and he walked it for the comfort that ghosts afford, and when the wind rose the dust drafted long furrows ahead of him as if some old plow were at work just under the skin of the earth and the world were being remade in silence. He saw a house once, roof fallen in and the chimney standing like a tooth, and on the steps a child's shoe sun-black and keeled with cracks, and he thought of a girl whose name he could not call back though he could see the angle of her ear and the way she had put her thumb to her lip when she listened and how she had not looked behind her when she crossed a threshold that had no door. He camped in a draw where ocotillo raised their green scourges and the dusk came down with the surety of a weight and there were moths at his fire that burnt their wings and slewed and lay there like ash come to life. He ate with his face to the dark as men will who have learned what the dark may hold and he did not pray because he had found prayer to be a transaction and the clerk at the window long since dead or quit, but he spoke a name that was not hers and not his and heard how small it was in the country of night. Text Passage: He came out of the west where the basalt lay like old fire gone to sleep and the sun lowered in a white wound and he walked with a stick he'd cut from a canyon willow and the dust on his boots took the day's last light and held it and let it go. He had no horse and no companion save the shadow that preceded him a little while and then failed him as all such friends will. Below lay an alkali flat where iron fenceposts leaned in attitudes of sorrow and the ragged wire held the skeletons of weeds as if the field had once contained some patient husbandry and now none. He climbed down into a wash cut in the earth like the memory of a river, the stone laid bare and planed smooth by a water that had departed and took with it all rumor of return, and in that chalk bed were the prints of coyotes and one print like a child's hand but longer, a cat that the sun had burned to string and bone somewhere out in the thorn. He walked until the hills behind him were blue as bruise and in the first of the evening he came upon a chapel of adobe that leaned into the wind with a kind of tired courage, its bell long gone and the whitewash flaked from its sides in scabs, and in the cool dark he found pews eaten with worm and a hymnbook furred with nests where paper was converted back to the formless. There had been a prayer written on the back wall with a stub of coal and the words were half erased by hands or rain O Lord remember the least of these and I will remember You and he stood looking at it and did not know if it was a vow or a bargain or both and if there were not some dark symmetry between the two. In the nave where the floor had sank he saw through a hole the hard earth and in it a slat box gone to powder and he squatted there with his hand to the lip as if a voice might rise from that poor ark and he whispered though to whom he could not say. Out in the scrub a wind came and went with a sound like something dragging chains and he stepped back into the little night and set a match to a twist of grass and held his tin cup over the flame with a patience as ancient as iron, the water in the cup no more than a spoonful that he had folded up from a seep at noon and saved against despair. Earlier that day he had crossed paths with a goatherd who'd said there was a spring east of the badland, not sweet but wet. East you say. East, the man had said, and he had looked at the distant dust the goats wrote upon the world and made no sign of blessing or farewell. He drank and tasted rust and stone and he sat and listened to the land go on with its mutterings and he thought that a man's life was not a story but a place, and the place was mostly night. Lightning walked the horizon and threw up a black tree against a brighter dark and in that brief accounting he thought he saw bones in the wash, a bull or a mule or a man it made no difference, the clean white rods laid out by the arithmetic of vultures. He slept with his coat under his head and when he woke the stars were still posted like nails hammered into a lid and a pale seam in the east told of the slow and certain unburial of the day and he rose and he took up his stick and he went on.

He followed a dry arroyo where the bed was scoured to chalk and old driftwood lay half buried like the bones of leviathans gone to powder, and the mule sniffed at the ground as if the ghost of water might yet lay its cool hand there. He carried a knife in a cracked leather sheath and a rope coiled tight and a tin cup and a small blue stone he kept in a pocket of his coat like a token against the long forgetting. He crossed a township that had gone to ruin and the houses leaned together as if in conspiracies of ash and weather, a single iron bed in the street with its springs rusted and sagging, a stovepipe fallen like a spent ramrod, and a church with the bell torn down and the ropes rotted and swallows nosing at the rafters. He went inside where the plaster was falling and the floor buckled and he found the ledger with its ink gone to shadows, names faded to the mere appearances of themselves, and he turned the leaves with his blackened thumb and saw the pages were thin and friable and soon they would go like leaves in the first hard wind. He came out and stood in the doorway and watched a rag of dust go cartwheeling down the street and he could hear in it the small teeth of grit and splinters, a dry song that has no kindness in it. At the edge of the town he found an old pumpjack nodding over a scar in the ground and the engine dead and the rods quiet and he put his hand on the iron and it was colder than truth. He moved on. At noon he stopped in the bed of a river where trickles of black seepage showed under a mat of reeds and he went to his knees and dug with his hands and the blood came up in small bright beads from the knuckles and the water came a little and he gave it to the mule and drank after and it tasted of stone and iron and long darkness. He slept with his back to a cottonwood charred by lightning and he dreamed a plain without edge and a road without end and a child walking backward with his hands to his ears against a sound that had not yet been made, and he woke and the stars were close enough to touch and yet they would not be touched and coyotes wrote their parables on the dark and no man would read them. In the morning he came upon a boy sitting on the lip of a culvert with his feet swinging above emptiness, a strip of red cloth tied round his wrist, and the boy watched him with the eyes of an animal that has known the trap and keeps the memory under its tongue, and the man nodded and put the blue stone in the boy's palm and the boy set it to his teeth and grinned without mirth and closed his fist upon it and the man moved on and did not look back. He walked under a white noon and the horizon pulled away as if in jest and the wind skinned the world to its plain facts, and in that subtraction there was a kind of truth and he bore it in silence and the mules' breath went in slow drafts and the land permitted no argument and so there was none.

Text Passage: In the gray of a day without promise the man came out upon the flats with the mule and the mule's shadow going before them long and black like some augury dragged across the salt and the wind was a pale hand that sifted the country and found in it nothing it much desired and the sky lay close and low and dead as old iron. He had slept in a draw among stones and the fire had died in a bowl of ash and he crushed the ash with his bootheel until it rose and whispered and settled again like a thing ashamed of itself. There was not a bird save a hawk hung at a great height like a nail driven in the dome of the world and even he at last turned and went away and the man reckoned this as counsel. The land had once gone under and come up bleached and scabbed and bitter and the crust broke underfoot and the brine shone and the mule laid back its ears and would not touch the little pools that lay in pans like mirrors to nothing. He carried a bundle tied with wire and in it the few proofs of his life and also a book without a cover and the pages were clotted with old rain and with a grit that had the taste of lye and he turned them now and then with the back of a finger as if for pain there were words to cure it. He named for himself the brief things he could lay claim to and the longer things that owned him and he spoke them softly so they would not see themselves and take offense, for it seemed to him that naming was a kind of theft and a kind of prayer and that most prayers were thefts poorly disguised and men called them providence because they did not wish to be alone with their pilfering. On the horizon a rise of dark earth like the back of some drowned beast and there an old mission slumped amid thorn and wire and the bell gone and the lintel burned and bats hung in the chancel like dry fruits and a bleached ladder lay in the dust and the rungs broke when he set his hand to them and he did not climb but stood in the nave without a roof and looked up into a heaven unadorned where the first star had come already like an ember no one could nurse back to flame. The mule stamped and there came out of the sacristy a coyote with a lantern's gaze and he watched it and it watched him and then it went and he listened to its soft tread scribe itself upon the earth and he imagined that the earth remembered all such lines and in the end would read them back and there would be no appeal. At evening a blow of cold ran down off the escarpment and set the salt to shining and the man walked on and his knee hurt him where an old mischief had lodged and would not confess and he let it preach what sermon it would and was not moved. He thought of a woman's hair in water and a child come up from a river with his eyes full of suns and he did not think long for there was no sense in digging a well in a place dry to the roots of the world and expecting sweet water to rise. Night gathered as if stitched up by unseen hands and he made no camp but crossed the flats with the stars coming forward each to its appointed post and the wind ran over the land like an animal without a name and he envied it.
