Text Passage: He went on along the white road where the caliche showed through and the grass lay burned to wire and the horizon sat like a blade and he felt in his bones the dumb arithmetic of miles and sun and whatever blood was left to him. The wind came off the flats and it had in it the taste of old fires and salt and a long dead sea and it set the mesquite to whispering as if the earth spoke to itself in sleep. He had a canteen slung from a strap and it knocked against his hip with a sound like the ticking of a blind clock and he counted by it without knowing he did. In the bar ditch a coyote lay with its jaw propped open and the flies walked that parched tongue like goldsmiths and the eyes were pearls of clouded glass and there was no more fear in the creature than in the stones. He passed a fence run out to nothing and the posts leaned like old penitents and the wire drew a line through the world that no beast nor man would own and he watched a dustdevil climb in the distance and go thin and break in the blue. The mountains were a rumor in the far light and at their feet lay a shoal of ruined cattle with their ribs stood up stark and bright and the big black birds shouldered among them and their shadows drew a raffle over the ground. At noon he came to a house that had been burned years gone and the chimneystone was scaled with soot and in the ash lay the buckles of a childs shoe green with verdigris and hard to the touch and he took it up and weighed it and set it down again and he said nothing for there was nothing to say to it. In the corner of the yard a cottonwood had survived and its leaves clicked like teeth and beyond it a dry acequia ran strait as a lance into the brush and he followed it for a time hoping for a seep or dark patch in the sand and there was none and he sat and drew his knife and split the hide on his heel and let the water in him out a little and stared at it and the ground drank. He slept and woke to the pale and meager light of a veiled sun and he dreamed in that sleep of a boy with a slate and a stub of chalk and the boy wrote his name and the name blew off the board as if it had been powder and the teacher took the boy by the wrist and led him into a field of white stones set in rows and told him to learn them for he would need to. In the evening he came to a wash and there was water moving there and it made a sound like the voice of something too remote to be concerned with men and he knelt and cupped it and drank and on the far bank a rattlesnake lay looped in a figure that seemed chosen and the head lifted and the tongue told the night what was to come and he rose and went on for he did not care to test what covenant might be offered. The first stars showed and they were cold and very old and he could not read them and he thought of gods that had no mouths and no eyes and whose commandments were given in drought and frost and in the fretted bark of trees and he felt a little lightness in him as if he were attended by something that was not quite mercy and not quite doom but kept pace with him on feet as soft as dust. He went on and the road bent and disappeared and came back again and he did not mark it and in the dark the whole country lay as if it waited upon him alone and he saw then in the faint starlight a moth come up out of the cracked earth where there was no flower nor stem and it beat at the air with its pale wings and climbed and was taken.

Text Passage: The road had no name and no charity and it went on among the wide flats where the earth had cracked open like old clay bowls and the light came up hard and pale off the rim of the world and found a man walking there with his coat tied up by a length of rope and the dust sat on him as if it had been made to fit him and the wind went dragging its sleeves across the salt. He carried a tin can that rang against his thigh and he had a book with the cover torn away that he kept in the lining of his coat and he did not read from it and did not pray from it and he spared it from the fire as a man might spare a stone. There were tracks of coyotes along the road and the small prints of a child that had not come back this way and there was a place where the storm had lifted a roof entire and set it down thirty paces off its house and the house stood open to the sky like a mouth that had forgotten speech. Far off the mountains lay as if hammered from iron and at noon they turned black and then blue and the heat went up in shimmers as if the ground were breathing. In the ditch lay the hull of a car stripped to its bones and the jack sagged slant in the loam and he put his hand on the metal and it was warm and then hot and he stepped back because even dead things can burn you. Toward evening he came upon a mule standing in a thicket of cane with its reins run between the stalks and the animal watched him with one good eye and the other a film of milk and it set its jaw and did not move and there was no sign of the hand that had tied it. He stood with it a while and the flies rose and fell and the sun went sliding between two narrow clouds as if passing through the slot of a door and he cut the rope and the mule did not follow and he did not ask it to. Night came with a brittle sound as of old paper and the stars appeared high and small and innumerable and he lay down beside the roadside cross that had been mounted out of lathe and he put his head near the wood and listened though crosses tell nothing and require nothing and dawn took him again. On the fourth day he reached a river like green glass and in the channel stones showed through with their backs scarred by long water and near the ford a fire ring and bones that were boiled to whiteness and a blackened pot with a flower nicked into its lip by some hand that had thought once of other things. He washed his face and the dust made paste on his cheeks and he looked down into the water at himself and he was no more than a shade passing under the slow sky and he thought of the men who had crossed before him with rifles and with songs and of how the earth kept no tally that any man could read. He stood and shouldered his coat and the book against his ribs was like the small heart of something he imagined still lived and he went on where the banks broke and the land rose and fell and every step gave back a little sound like words he could not afford to say.

He had passed through a field where the mesquite was burned to black spines and the fenceline was a wire hung on charred uprights and in the ash were cattle prints crisp as pottery and nothing living to claim them and a steer skull propped at an angle like it had turned to hear some last dim order and would not tell it. Out a ways the ground opened to an arroyo and he stood and watched it and the thin water in it was the color of tea left to die in a cup and when the wind leaned into that cut it sounded like a throat with a stone in it. The man took a drink and the water tasted of iron and of the ruin of long buried things and he felt it go down and settle like a lie. He had no company save a carrion bird that slid in the high air on black boards of wing and the bird watched him with that old and sterile regard held by things that have outlived all naming and the man raised a hand and the bird did not fear and the world went on unrebuked. He found a corral of leaning poles and a roofless shack with the door swung from one hinge and a well with its rope grayed and chafed and a bucket hammered thin as a pilgrim's alms. He lowered the bucket and the pulley complained in a tired old voice and the water came up rank and mineral and he drank and let the horse drink and stood there listening to nothing until even the nothing had a sound to it as of cloth being folded in some far room. Carrion birds hung upon the air in a slow and pondered circle and somewhere a coyote gave out with its moldy laugh and the laugh had no humor in it but the world knew it and answered with silence. He gathered roots of mesquite and a board from a broken crate and walled a small fire from the wind and ate hard bread and a strip of sinewed meat and he watched the smoke go thin and colorless into the high blue like the last prayer of a man who believes without hope. A snake came in from the dark and the fire put a brass upon its eye and he took an iron peg from the shack door and pinned the head quick and cut the neck with a short blade and skinned it and turned the pale meat on the coals and the flesh sang and flared and he ate and there was grease on his lip and ash on his hands and he felt no better and no worse for the killing of a thing that would have killed him wrong or right. Night set down like a lid and stars came up by the million and lay in their appointed places and the sheer press of them seemed to him an old and unmerciful order into which men moved for a time as sparks drifted upward and vanished upon the black. He passed a fence of wire that had sunk to the posts and a cross of bar iron planted in the marl and a name once chiseled upon a stone and the wind had unlearned it. He saw there the sign of a small thing gone before him, a child's heel pressed in the bed of the stream and the sawtooth track of a dog alongside and further up the banks the wider tread of men in old shoes, the heels sloped down at the corners, and he thought how a road is not always a thing fixed to the earth but comes and goes in the mind and in the courage of those who set foot upon it. The sky was hammered tin and the sun climbed out of the blue reach and took up its work and the heat came like a lid and the snakes went into the cracks and the lizards lay still and glass eyed upon the stones and all things waited. He moved on and by midmorning he came upon a length of fence drooped in a sag and in the snarl of wire there was a coydog that had fought until it had twisted itself near in two and it lay with its flanks going in little increments and a gray tongue gone to leather and it looked at him with the ruined vacancy that the world puts upon its creatures when it has done with them. He stood above it and the flies got up and set down in a dark shifting and he took a rock and he did what was to be done and the body spasmed once and was still and he set his boot on the Tpost and wrenched the wire free and coiled it like something sleeping and he laid the dog in the shade of a greasewood and covered its head with an old burlap he kept and he took off his hat and set it in the crook of his elbow and the wind went over him as if to empty him and then it was quiet. A machine by the door gives you a number that is instantly the most important fact about you, and you sit on a row of plastic chairs that force your spine into a position of repentance. Overhead a screen scrolls little sentences in friendly type, all of them grammatical and all of them lies; in the corners the cameras blink patiently, like cats who have learned not to expect much from people. Everybody carries a folder. It is always the same folder, a grey thing that bulges at the corners where reality refuses to lie flat. There is an old woman whose purse has the polished look of something handled to the bone; there is a thin man with the blue tattoos that poor men collect as boys; a girl who could not be more than twenty has brought a pushchair that drips crumbs like a distress signal. When a number is called a small bustle happens, and then there is the thud of the stamp, which is the only sound in the room that has any conviction in it. You are never asked what you need; you are asked what you can prove. They want proofs of existence that you should not have had to hoard: letters stamped by vanished offices, bills addressed to addresses you no longer occupy, certificates that were never certificates of anything but the appetite of the state. Photocopies are not acceptable, though they themselves live by photocopies. Meanwhile a poster on the far wall tells you that fraud costs us all, and the smiling couple on it are the sort of people who never come to places like this except to be photographed. I had come on my fatherÃ¢ÂÂs errand because he is no longer steady on his legs and because there are some battles he will not fight now that he is taught by pain. At the desk the woman with the stamp is not a bad person, though I did not like her. She has had to train a certain tendon of the face so that compassion does not spoil the inkpad. She tells me that the forms have changed, and then, a minute later, that they have not changed but have been clarified. Her power lies in refusing to understand. A vending machine sells tea that tastes like a summary of defeat. It gives no change. They have spent a great deal of public money on the new logo; somewhere a presentation was given in which somebody said that a modern look builds trust. Text Passage: At the Fuel Office the queue began before daylight, a dark rope of people knotted round two corners and along the wall where the plaster scabbed off in little flakes; the smell in the line was of wet wool, damp paper and that sour, faintly burnt odour left by bad coal, an odour that clung to the city as persistently as soot clings to a window frame. Thomas had brought his cup of tea with him in an enamel mug whose rim was chipped, and the tea had already acquired the taste of tin and cold air, but he held it two-handed as if any small source of warmth was to be honoured. A little loudspeaker, fixed high under the eaves and protected by a cone of wire-netting, crackled and then delivered a woman's voice, educated and impersonal, announcing a "temporary adjustment of household allocations due to improved efficiency targets," and this sentence, which was repeated twice with a few variations in the order of the words, moved slowly over the queue like a thin sheet of rain no one could avoid. It was always like this in such places: posters inside the glass case showed a smiling woman in a bright kitchen, sleeves rolled up, with a neat pile of coal beside her and a child warming his hands as if fires were conjured out of good behaviour and slogans, while the real women stood here with scarves over their hair, coughing into their palms and shifting their feet because the cold went through boots as if leather were a polite pretence. When at last the doors were unbolted the press forward was not a rush, merely the stubborn shuffle of people who had learned to put each foot where the person in front had left space, and at the counter the clerks sat in their coats with the collars up, each at a desk furnished with a rubber stamp, an inkpad, a ledger and a stack of forms; and though their hands were red and the ink thickened in the bottle, the stamping was brisk and final, a small, single rap that sounded like a gavel dismissing appeals. Thomas spelled his name; the clerk did not look up but his mouth tightened on a pencil. "You received full issue last month," he said, as if that were a favour wasted. "Two adults, one child," Thomas said, keeping his voice flat. "One adult, one dependent," said the clerk, tapping the ledger. One did not look at the slogan for long. One kept one's eyes on the floorboards, which had been polished to a greasy shine by shoes more obedient than any brush, and one considered the little dance that was required at the front, the brief kneel before the stool where the clerk sat with his sleeves rolled, his biro leaking blue into the creases of his hand. He addressed each applicant in the same neutral, impersonal way, as if reading the inscriptions on stones: Name, Address, Reason for Application, Declaration of Gratitude. From a loudspeaker in the corridor a man's voice, thick with phlegm and confidence, announced the usual figures: production up by five percent, wastage reduced, a triumph of coordination. It is strange how numbers can make a man feel poorer. The clerk, who had the thin, sharp face of an underfed ferret, stamped my paper with a square wooden block and pushed a chipped cup of brown liquid towards me across the counter, my allotted refreshment. It had the taste of tannin and tin, and as I swallowed it I felt the curious steadiness that comes when one has performed a distasteful act correctly and is at liberty to think no more about it. Behind me a man in a coat that had been new three winters ago said, in a calm voice, that his mother could not climb the stairs any more; in front of me a girl in cheap cosmetics asked twice whether the coupon would be valid next week. The buses came in a slow procession, breathing their thin smoke on the people who stood beside the shelter with the patience of cattle, and the hoardings opposite wore their complicated smiles: Be Alert, Do Your Part, WeÃ¢ÂÂre All in This Together. There is a stale odour that grows in such places, a blend of disinfectant and stewed vegetables, and it seems to rise from the very paving stones, as if the stones themselves had been lectured into cleanliness. I watched a girl in a cheap coat counting coins with her thumb and forefinger, and the act, which ought to be private, took place in plain sight because the habit of privacy has been argued out of everyone. A man with a plastic badgeÃ¢ÂÂSecurity Support, it said, not SecurityÃ¢ÂÂwandered up and down with the conscientious air of a boy pretending to be his father. He had a list in his hand and ticked things off in a manner that conveyed the satisfaction of obedience. The list did not look at him, and the bus did not look at anyone; it merely opened its mouth, took us in, and shut it. The windows were scratched with initials and messages, and if you took the trouble to read them you found they were not messages at all, only the crude gestures people make when they are allowed no better language. Opposite me a labourer with damp shoulders nodded in and out of sleep, and each time the bus jolted he clutched at his lunch tin as if it were a testimony no prosecutor could shake. In the bus queue the men stood with their tin lunch boxes and their tired eyes, and the women held string bags that had learned to keep their shape even when there was nothing in them. Posters at the tram stop advised us to share, to save, to keep our lips buttoned and our backs straight. In the office it was a world of blotters and ink-stains and two steel filing cabinets that always smelled faintly of glue. The calendar showed a smiling farmhand gathering up sheaves under a sky the colour of toothpaste; the real sky, visible in a slice between roofs, was the old city sky, yellowish as tea. Collins, our supervisor, had red knuckles and boots that had been polished with a devotion usually reserved for the dead; he was not a cruel man, only a practical one, and he had learned to speak of rules as if they were facts of nature. He would rest a square finger on a column of figures and say, without looking up, that the totals must show not what we had, but what we intended to have, Ã¢ÂÂfor alignment.Ã¢ÂÂ We altered the columns in neat pencil strokes, erasing carefully so that the paper would not burr; each individual number told no lies, but they learned to sing in unison soon enough. And yet the city offered its consolations in penny form: a bakery smell unscrolling from a basement door; a cat enthroned on a window ledge like a general; a slap of sudden sun on a corrugated roof. At noon the canteen stew came in bowls whose rims were perpetually greasy, the gravy thin as varnish and studded with islands of fat that trembled with every step. We ate and spoke of nothing in particular, or rather we spoke at length around the names of the things that pinched. The afternoon was a procession of forms: APPROVED, RECEIVED, DUPLICATE; the stamp thudded like a small heartbeat. I used to think that the worst part of lying was the wickedness of it; later I saw it was its ease. It did not require us to invent a story; it required us only to be tired. Text Passage: In the still hour, when the pale morning, like a modest scholar, enters the world without clamour, I have mused upon the pitiable economy by which minds are trained to be dependent where they might be free; for it has been my constant observation that the very beings most sedulously instructed to please are the least empowered to act, and that the wreaths woven for their brows shrink, on trial, to cords for their hands. It is not that Nature has denied them strength or noble curiosityÃ¢ÂÂno, she has scattered in every breast seeds of fortitude and of just ambitionÃ¢ÂÂbut a base system of discipline waters only those that shoot into showy foliage, and kills the roots of virtue for want of exercise. Children are soothed into docility with sugared phrases, and when they are grown they are still rocked by the same lullaby, recast into the soft cadences of gallantry; thus they are kept quiet, as if reason were a fretful babe to be stilled with toys. But who, that has an eye to the ends of existence, can be satisfied that a creature capable of comprehending truth should be content to sparkle and vanish like a firefly in a summer garden? And shall we, who boast of light, continue to kindle our daughtersÃ¢ÂÂ lamps only that they may shine across a ball-room floor, and not that they may read the page of life with composure? I would have them learn to reverence duty before decoration, to practise justice at home that they may judge it abroad, and to understand that tenderness is enfeebled, not exalted, when it is unaccompanied by self-command. Yet, whilst I contend for this severer culture, I do not banish grace; I only demand that it should be the handmaid of sense, and not her imperious mistress. A woman who has formed the habit of weighing evidence, of subduing caprice by principle, will not, I am persuaded, be a less faithful friend, a less affectionate mother, because she is more a rational creature; on the contrary, the affections, released from the tyranny of whim and fear, expand with a steadier warmth, as the hearth gives a securer glow when the wind of accident is not suffered to scatter the flame. If any plead fashion against me, I ask by what authority that painted idol exacts homage? If by long prescription, then despotism might claim antiquity for its charter; if by consent, then let consent be informed, not extorted by ridicule or bribed by vanity. Mothers, who tremble to see a brow knit in thought, yet smile at a blush won by a foolish compliment, are raising not companions for virtue but victims for satiety; and men, who complain that frivolity wearies them, forget that they rewarded it yesterday as a cheap diversion. Shall we perpetually mistake smoothness for peace and silence for contentment, and then wonder that the first storm discovers a wreck beneath the flowers? I would rather behold a girl stumbling over the rough stones of inquiry than gliding, with practised step, to the music of approbation; for the former, though she bruises her foot, acquires a firmer tread, and the latter, though she seems to fly, has no wings when the tune is broken. Let us, then, restore to education its dignity, teach both sexes to venerate truth as the only ornament that does not tarnish, and we may yet see domestic happiness built not on concealment but on confidence, and public virtue sustained by private integrity; for the heart that has learned to respect itself will not easily bow to any idol, whether named pleasure, opinion, or power.

What wonder, then, if, excluded from the invigorating air of truth and labour, they become artful rather than wise, tender in nerves yet hard in vanity, quick to resent a shade of neglect and slow to feel a great duty? I blush for the hollow gallantry that bows before a cap while it neglects a mind; and I tremble lest the bloom so carefully cherished should fade into an early winter, leaving no harvest of understanding to sustain the heart. Let us be plain: the grand business of education is to cultivate reason, to teach the judgment to stand upon its own centre, and to render the passions the ministers, not the masters, of conduct; and this business, which we admit to be obligatory for men, is with perverse consistency denied to women, as if Providence had endowed them with souls merely to echo back a fashionable sentiment. I ask not that they govern men, but that they learn to govern themselves; not that they usurp employments for which they have no calling, but that no honest employment be closed against them because it demands firmness of principle and patience of thought. Modesty, if it be more than a veil for indolence, must spring from self-respect; and self-respect will never grow in a soil watered only by flattery. Text Passage: I have often observed, in those assemblies where idle magnificence and unmeaning smiles usurp the name of politeness, that the human character, which might be raised by strenuous exertion into a noble simplicity, is frittered away into pretty fragments of behaviour; and I confess it has awakened in me a sorrowful indignation, not at the sex alone on whom the masque is chiefly fastened, but at the men who contrive the pageant and then affect to be disgusted by its hollowness. What a pitiful circle, where desire is inflamed by the very weakness it pretends to pity, and where dependence is decked out like a virtue, that the more securely it may bind! I would ask, with that plainness which truth authorizes, wherein lies the dignity of beings who are taught to practise a servile address instead of cultivating an upright mind? Better, surely, to be roughly sincere than delicately false; better to hazard the censure of fools than to invite it by purchasing their favour with a smile. The faculties of the soul are instruments too precious to be tuned only to the small tinklings of gallantry; they demand exercise, labour, and a scope that grows with use; for the understanding, like a limb, withers if it be swathed, and strength of character, like freedom, is not bestowed but earned. I am weary of hearing that taste is a womanÃ¢ÂÂs empire, and the toilette her senate; for what dominion is it that melts at the first breath of infirmity, or what legislation that trembles before a wrinkle? Those who would have us believe that a graceful pliancy supplies the place of fortitude confound the shadow with the substance; they make of life a puppet-show, and of society a nursery where moral giants are expected to spring from cradles. Let woman, then, be received into the commonwealth of reason, not as a pet to be indulged nor as a cynic to be feared, but as a fellow-creature accountable for her actions, whose virtue is enlightened by principles and sustained by habits. Habits, I say, not caprices; a steady industry that tempers fancy, and a plain sincerity that rebukes the vanity of show. We shall not build a durable happiness upon cushions, nor rear citizens under garlands; the hour of trial will strip off every borrowed feather, and then, alas! how naked will appear that character which has trusted to paint and posture. It is time to cease praising the sickly bloom of sensibility that faints at a duty and revives at a compliment. Truth is not the enemy of grace, but its stern parent; and charity itself becomes a pernicious indulgence when it protects indolence at the expense of improvement. I would have mothers learn, that they may teach; wives think, that they may advise; daughters strive, that they may stand; and men, if they love truly, prove it by desiring companions in virtue, not playthings in leisure. Thus, by disciplining the heart through the mind, and fortifying the affections by directing them to what is permanent, we might at last exchange the glitter of a morning dew for the calm light of day, and find in the sober exercise of our powers that joy which no accident can tarnish and no fashion can recall.

If men would be truly honoured in the domestic circle, let them cease to rear idols to be worshipped by caprice and nourished by caprice; let them rather cultivate companions, whose affection can survive the bloom of youth because it is rooted in esteem. For can a union be called sacred where one party is educated to please and the other to command? Where the conversation is a string of pretty nothings, and the hearth, which should be the school of virtue, becomes the nursery of vanity? I ask, is it generous to reward a woman for her helplessness and then reproach her with it, to place the cup of knowledge to her lips and dash it away because the draught might give strength as well as sweetness? To render a creature pleasing is not to render her virtuous; nay, to decorate a prison with garlands is still to confess it a prison. The heart, made the plaything of vanity, will never rise to that fortitude which, amid prosperity, preserves simplicity, and, in adverse fortune, remains calm without affectation. It is not that I would extinguish the graceful charities that soften our existence; but I maintain that tenderness, to be pure, must spring from strength, and that strength can have no root save in enlightened principles. I met, in my walk, a countrywoman bearing a pail with a firm step and a clear, composed eye; her hands, though browned by honest work, looked more dignified than the jewelled fingers I have seen twitch with the fever of vanity; and I confess, with a delight that may seem rustic to the votaries of fashion, that the health of her labour, the self-possession of her manner, conveyed more instruction to me than a dozen sentimental homilies addressed to the female heart. Text Passage: When I consider the rapidity with which the blossoms of youth are shed, and the calculating industry with which society trains young women to value those frail flowers beyond the enduring fruits of the understanding, I cannot forbear to protest, with all the energy that a love of truth inspires, against a system which mistakes glitter for light, and submission for virtue; for what can be more pernicious than to substitute a parade of delicacy for the genuine cultivation of the mind, or to foster a sensibility so exquisite that it trembles at effort and recoils from duty, while the faculties that might sustain the burden of life are left unused, like instruments rusting in their cases? I am not insensible to the innocent graces of manner, nor to the tender charities that soften domestic existence; but when these are elevated into the grand end of female education, when mothers, themselves tutored to court estimation by compliance rather than merit, teach their daughters to measure worth by the smiles they can evoke and the gauds they can purchase, then do we behold a whole sex fashioned into masksÃ¢ÂÂamiable, perhaps, and even engaging, yet incapable of a steady attachment to principle, because unexercised in that severer discipline which alone confirms the habits of virtue. Do you accuse women of trifling? Yet what serious occupation have you allowed them? Do you lament their caprice? Text Passage: It has long appeared to me a pernicious sophistry, industriously propagated by those who profit from the mental imbecility of their dependents, that delicacy is the chief ornament of a woman, and passive obedience the most persuasive form of wisdom; for what is delicacy, when sifted to the bran, but a timid shrinking from the exercise of judgment, a disguise for ignorance; and what is obedience, when unexamined, but the abdication of that very faculty which constitutes us moral agents? Shall we then continue to substitute the flutter of affected sensibility for the steady energy of virtue, and call it refinement because it trembles rather than acts? Custom, that hoary tyrant to whom even reason too often bends, has for centuries wrapped the female mind in swaddling clothes of ceremony; it has bound her limbs with ribbons and named the bandage grace; it has locked her faculties in a gilded cage and styled the bars protection; yet do not the very feathers that deck the prisoner fall into disorder at the slightest gust, while the unadorned pinions, nerved by use, cleave the common air with purpose and composure? I am weary of hearing that frivolous accomplishments nourish the heart, or that a head well stored with truth must chill affection; love itself, if it be not anchored in principle, is but a fever that wastes what it warms, and the smile that wins today, unfortified by duty, shall tomorrow betray. Let us then demand, not as a caprice but as a debt to human nature, that girls and boys be trained to the same sovereign allegianceÃ¢ÂÂto reason; not parceled out, as if by divine charter, into franchises of thought for the one and pantomimes of feeling for the other; for the household is but the nursery of the state, and those who would have citizens just and magnanimous must not first fashion their earliest instructors vain and servile. If modesty be a virtue (and I grant it, when it guards truth rather than hides it), it will not be found in the art of flattering power, nor in the pretty bashfulness that makes a jest of duty, but in the fortitude that dares to be simple amid ostentation, and to speak plainly where folly has decreed a cipher. You talk of female influence, and point to drawing-rooms where the air is perfumed with adulation, as if the incense proved a sanctuary; yet I ask, what benefit descends to the common good from lips trained to please, not to persuade; from hands practiced in the dance, but unacquainted with the ledger of household justice; from minds dressed like windows for a holiday, transparent and vacant, admitting every idle gaze but reflecting no interior order? No: true dignity is the child of self-government; and self-government is learned, as every hardy virtue is learned, by exercise and exposureÃ¢ÂÂby grappling with difficulties, by tasting the wholesome bread of industry, by resisting the quick seductions of applause, and by preferring the solid peace that attends duty to the glittering misery that dogs vanity. I would not unsex woman; I would unchain her. Bid her cultivate the understanding, and her affections will grow more faithful, not less; allow her to be a companion, and she will be a more reverent wife, a more intelligent mother, a citizen in soul though the laws are tardy to acknowledge the title; and then perhaps we shall no longer hear the paltry cant that weakness is lovely, nor witness the melancholy spectacle of immortal beings trained to seek importance in littleness, and to barter the birthright of reason for a smile that dies with the season.

Text Passage: Walking at dawn through the narrow streets, where the first light, as if modest of its influence, touched only the uppermost panes and cornices, I could not but reflect, with mingled tenderness and severity, on the slumbering faculties of those who would soon throng the ways, decked to please and disciplined to obey; for what avails the elasticity of youth, or the treasuries of sensibility, if their owner be taught to distrust the steady hand of reason, and to accept, in lieu of substantial freedom, the toys of preeminence and the tinkling adulation of ignorance? The mothers, I am told, labour to make their daughters amiable, and the fathers, with equal zeal, endeavour to see them established; yet in that term, establishment, what a dreary constellation of calculations is contained, as if happiness were a sum to be cast upon a slate rather than a virtue to be cultivated in the heart. They decorate the mind with a few accomplishments, adorning the windows while the foundation rots, and then, having fitted the creature for a show, retire self-satisfied, as though the ornaments of a puppet could impart the principle of life. Ought we not rather to insist, calmly yet inflexibly, that a rational being can neither love nor be loved with dignity who has not learned to respect herself as a creature destined for improvement, accountable to conscience, and allied, by the common charter of humanity, to the exercise of independent judgment? I have seen a young woman, her eyes brilliant with unexpended thought, taught to bend that native fire into a timid compliance with the hourly caprice of fashion, till her very sentiments, once robust and wholesome, grew as flaccid as the ribbon that confined her hair; and I have pitied, more than blamed, the man who, believing himself master, found he had embraced only a glittering shadow, which could not sustain his respect nor outlast the novelty of possession. What is it that renders friendship noble, but the free commerce of frank spirits? Yet how cruelly do we depart from this simple harmony, when we fashion beings, chiefly women, to flutter not like the lark but to languish like a tendril trained round a gilded prop, catching transient gleams without ever meeting the source of light. If the understanding be the lamp of the soul, and virtue the calm flame it should invigorate, why are we so solicitous to shade it with the gauze of frivolous acquirements, or to teach the hand to scatter sweet odours that flatter the senses whilst the mind starves? The very language of politeness which so many parade as the essence of female excellence is too often the varnish laid upon obsequiousness; and those tender emotions, lauded as the sign of a pure heart, prove, when detached from principle, but the quick vapours that, rising from a heated imagination, soon condense into tears and caprices. Shall we then persist in educating half the human race to be incapable of governing themselves, and afterwards wonder that the other half grow petulant despots in their turn? No: call it not order when it rests upon the abduction of liberty; name it not virtue when it springs from fear. If, instead of decking the girl in chains of silk, we entrusted her early with the wholesome tools of thoughtÃ¢ÂÂaccustoming her to weigh motives, to trace consequences, and to reverence truth, not authorityÃ¢ÂÂwhat coquetry would survive the habit of sincerity? Love would become the companion of respect, and domestic life, instead of a theatre for petty stratagems, would be a school of mutual improvement. I am not insensible to the blandishments of affection, nor insensible to the sacred softness that makes the hearth a sanctuary; yet tenderness, when it crouches at the footstool of caprice, is but an idolatry of self, and the docility that is extolled in the sex is frequently a mute folly, smiling whilst it betrays. Give me rather the woman who dares to examine before she yields, who feels because she knows, and who, planting her heart upon a steady principle, can weather the gusts of passion without bending to every murmuring breeze. For what avails a bloom that fades with the season, if it never bore a fruit to sustain another? If a mother desire a daughter truly amiable, let her first desire her truly honest; if she would have her graceful, let her bid her be just; for the upright spirit, accustoming itself to respect reality more than appearance, will find a posture for the body that cannot be aped by the practised coquette, and a tone for the voice that no mimic can counterfeit. Text Passage: Contending for the dignity of human nature, I rest my plea upon this plain but neglected axiom, that moral beings are bound to cultivate the powers with which they are endowed, for without the discipline of reason, virtue is but a pageant, and obedience the habit of a slave. If, then, you confine women to a round of frivolous employments, and teach them to prize ornament above understanding, do you not secretly sap the foundations of public felicity? The character of a nation is the offspring of its households; and can you expect firmness in the citizen, or elevation in the magistrate, when the first nurse of his sentiments has been tutored to shrink from inquiry, to tremble before authority, and to mistake compliance for benevolence? Tell me, I entreat you, by what charter man assumes to himself the office of final judge of female capacity, while he seals their books and bars their rostrum; is not this, under the specious name of protection, an usurpation of the prerogatives of rational creatures? Text Passage: When I survey the manners of my country, and behold how the bloom of female life is bartered away for the brittle coin of applause, I am constrained to ask whether we have mistaken glitter for light, and gentility for virtue; for the very discipline that is said to refine our sex does, in truth, reduce us to a nervous dependence, wherein caprice passes for delicacy and silence for humility, while the stern yet salutary labours of reason are dismissed as masculine intrusions upon a sphere consecrated to ornament. We are taught to govern by a smile what we have never been allowed to govern by principle; and thus the nursery becomes a little court, the drawing-room a little theatre, where trifles rise to prerogatives, and sincerity retires abashed before the pageant of studied softness. I speak not as an enemy to gentleness, nor as a votary of coarse usurpation; I would have women mild because they are strong, and tender because they are just, their affections the handmaids, not the jailers, of their judgment. Grant us, then, the honest exercise of our understandings; accustom us to the wholesome friction of truth; oblige us to render a reason for our choices; and you will soon perceive that our gaiety will cease to be a fever of vanity and become the serenity of self-possession. For what is freedom but the power to obey law which the conscience recognises? and what is virtue but the steady habit of preferring what deserves preference? Yet while we are schooled to pant for admiration as the sickly child pants for sugared draughts, the staple of our being is consumed by cravings never satisfied, and our very charms become the chains that fret us. Nor do men escape unscathed from this traffic of illusions: he who is flattered by a puppet must himself become a player; he who would be loved for dominion will be obeyed without esteem; and the commerce of mutual deceit impoverishes both, even as it glitters with counterfeit wealth. Let there be instead a frank covenant between rational creatures, owning the same origin and accountable to the same tribunal. If you fear that study will make us vain, give us truth enough to shame conceit; if you dread that toil will harden us, vary our tasks, and let exercise brace the limbs while conversation braces the mind; if you suspect that piety will dwindle when it walks without trinkets, then entrust it to solitude and work, where it thrives. Educate a woman to be a companion, and you add a citizen to the state; educate her to be a bauble, and you forge, with your own soft hands, a chain for posterity. Text Passage: At noon the wind came up off the salt pan and went through the weeds with a sound like paper burning and he stood with his hat held down and saw the land laid out to the compass points like a thing cut and flensed and left to dry. The mule shifted and laid back its ears and he spoke to it without moving his mouth as if the words themselves might cost more breath than he could spare. The road was a long chalk scar on the earth and in the ruts were the imprints of old shoes and the cloven clefts of cattle that had gone on into the glare and not come back and he stepped in none of them for fear of taking on their fates. He had a sack tied with rawhide and in it a skillet and a coil of wire and a Bible without a cover and he could not say where he had got the book or when, only that it had found him like a windblown paper that would not be shaken off. The town when he came to it was a congregation of boards and boltheads and he stood in the doorway of the store and called but no one answered, the dust slanting in the light like the slow fall of some pale rain that nourished nothing. He took what was not nailed and what was nailed he left and that was the law. He found a tin with peaches printed on the side and a knife whose edge had been worked down to a silver smile and he cut open the tin and drank the syrup and closed his eyes upon its coldness and when he opened them there was a dog at the threshold, a brindled cur whose ribs numbered like a ledger, and it watched him without trust or hatred as if he were a weather that must be borne. He held out the lid with the syrup shining in it and the dog took one step and then another and its tongue was black and delicate as a mothwing and it lapped and drew back. He could see where the dog had been laying in the corner by the old sacks and there the fleas rose up like dark foam at his boots. He spoke again and the sound of his voice in that empty house was a thing separate from him and unowned. Toward evening he led the mule to the church to get out of the quartering wind and there were bats nested in the rafters and he could hear them moving like a drycloth shaken in a distant room. The altar had been dragged and the muslin torn away and behind it was a crude door that went down to some root cellar and he stood at the threshold and listened and there came up to him the slow seep of the earth itself, a sound like water speaking to stone. He knew then the well they had sunk under the church, to keep it from thieves and travelers and God, and he lowered the coil of wire and it found nothing but the taste of cold. Text Passage: By the time the wind laid down the dust kept moving of its own accord and the man came off the flat like a pilgrim walking the floors of some dead house and his boots were white as bone from the caliche and his hat carried a margin of sun like a seal. He bore a canvas sack and a tin dipper and a knife in a cracked sheath and he went on through the sparse mesquite and past the husked ocotillo spires that looked like the fingers of a drowned god and there were wires drawn taut between posts where no fence was needed and the wires sang and the earth under them had been scalloped by the passage of cattle who were gone from the country long before. He came upon the remains of a house that the wind had razed without touching and the sheetiron roof was lifted at one corner beating like a clock and there were charred plates of wallboard propped in angles and a stove made all of rivets and black enamel and in the stove a bird had nested and flown and the nest lay rimmed with ash like a relic. He set down his sack and went in and the floor sighed and the light fell through the ribs of the rafters and a calendar hung to a nail and the saint upon it wore a ring of unburnt whiteness about the face where the smoke could not cling and the halo was the color of new brass and the eyes were rubbed away by the years. He found a photograph in a frame and the glass was filmed with dust and the men and women stood against a painted cloud and their clothes were simple and their mouths were small as if they had sworn something and kept it and when he turned the picture the paper lifted from the backboard with a long soft tear like skin. Outside the crows moved down in a black alphabet and their letters meant nothing and the creekbed ran chalk and thorn and you could see where the floods had written their brief scripture in the silt and departed and everywhere the sun laid its hand the world took the brand without complaint. Toward evening he heard the growl of a truck and it came over the marl with a pulse like a beast's heart and two men got down in hats that seemed too small for the great expanse of sky and they saw him and said nothing and he said nothing and they moved into the ruins and their boots made a cracking like ice and one of them lifted the stovetop with his hands and let it fall and the noise went out to the low hills and did not return. The man drank from his dipper and the water tasted of tin and eons and when they came out again one of them watched him as if he were a question he did not want to be asked and then they climbed back into the truck and backed and turned and left a hanging plume that the evening wind drew into skeins and threadbare veils. The first star burned through like a coal in paper and by night he had a fire against a rockface and he warmed his hands and there came to him the scent of creosote and old rain and he slept and in his sleep he saw a sea where no sea could be and the waves came smithereening along a shore of skulls and he woke to the sound of nothing at all and the ashes of the fire made a slow constellation of their own. He rose before dawn and shouldered his sack and went on and his shadow walked ahead of him long and patient as a guide and the east was bloodless and then it was thinly veined and then it bled and the birds spoke in tongues of iron and all about him the country opened without limit and without favor and took him in.
